about: The Sudan IMNCI course (classic, face-to-face course) as self-study lessons: Module 1 Introduction, Module 2 Assess and classify the sick child age 2 months up to 5 years, Module 3 Identify treatment, Module 4 Treat the child, Module 5 Counsel the mother, Module 6 Management of the sick young infant, Module 7 Follow-up (Sudan National Child Health Program books, 2023). Photographs come from the IMNCI photograph booklet in Protocol management. The book text is kept word for word, in the order and with the activities of the facilitator guide (December 2021): demonstrations and facilitator points as notes, drills as flip cards, exercises in the exercise manager. Videos are placeholders until the narration is recorded.

sections.title: Why integrated case management?

read.text: Explain why a sick child's illnesses are managed together, with one set of integrated guidelines.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Welcome to the IMNCI course
read.caption: Watch this first. The narration is being recorded.

read.text: Think first: pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles and malnutrition together cause what share of deaths in children under five years of age?
read.explanation: Pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, and malnutrition cause more than 70% of deaths in children under five years of age.

read.text: INTRODUCTION

Pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, and malnutrition cause more than 70% of deaths in children under five years of age. There are feasible and effective ways that health workers in clinics can care for children with these illnesses and prevent most of these deaths. WHO & UNICEF used updated technical findings to describe management of these illnesses in a set of integrated (combined) guidelines, instead of separate guidelines for each illness. They then developed this training package to teach the integrated case management process to health workers who see sick children.

Health workers have experience treating common childhood illnesses. They are often trained using separate, disease-specific guidelines, such as guidelines for treating malaria, or guidelines for managing diarrhoea. However, they may have difficulty combining different guidelines when caring for a sick child with several problems. They may not know which problems are most important to treat. With limited time and drugs, health workers may not be able to identify and treat all of a sick child’s problems. There are important relationships between the illnesses. For example, repeated diarrhoeal episodes often lead to malnutrition; diarrhoea, which often accompanies or follows measles, is particularly severe. Therefore, effective case management needs to consider all of a child’s symptoms.

read.title: How the illnesses are linked

cards.front: Diarrhoea that accompanies or follows measles

cards.back: needs to consider all of a child's symptoms.

read.text: A health worker can follow the integrated case management process taught in this course to quickly consider all of a child’s symptoms and not overlook any problems. The health worker can determine if a child is severely ill and needs urgent referral. If not, the health worker can follow the guidelines to treat the child’s illnesses. The guidelines also describe counseling for mothers and other caretakers.
A health worker follows the integrated case management process. What can they determine first?
options: Whether the child is severely ill and needs urgent referral
Which single disease the child has
read.explanation: The health worker can determine if a child is severely ill and needs urgent referral. If not, the health worker can follow the guidelines to treat the child's illnesses. The guidelines also describe counseling for mothers and other caretakers.

read.text: The case management guidelines incorporate existing WHO guidelines, such as those for managing diarrhoeal disease, acute respiratory infections, malaria, and for immunization. In this course, health workers will see how the disease-specific guidelines fit into a more comprehensive and efficient process for management of a sick child.

The case management guidelines describe how to care for a child who presents at a clinic with an illness for the first time or for a scheduled follow-up visit to check the child’s improvement. They address most but not all of the major reasons a child is brought to a clinic for illness. A child returning with chronic problems or less common illnesses may require special care, which is not described in this course. The course does not describe the management of trauma or other acute emergencies due to accidents or injuries.
Is it described in this course? Sort each one the way the book says.

items.text: A child who comes to the clinic with an illness for the first time
A scheduled follow-up visit to check the child's improvement
A child returning with chronic problems or less common illnesses that need special care
Trauma or other acute emergencies due to accidents or injuries

read.explanation: The guidelines address most but not all of the major reasons a child is brought to a clinic for illness.

read.text: Although AIDS is not addressed specifically, the case management guidelines address the most common reasons children with HIV seek care: diarrhoea and respiratory infections. When a child who is believed to have HIV presents with any of these common illnesses, he can be treated like any child coming in with the illness for the first time. If a child’s illness does not respond to the standard treatments taught in this course, or if a child becomes severely malnourished, or returns to the clinic repeatedly, he is referred to a hospital for special care. This results in children with AIDS being referred.
A child believed to have HIV is brought with diarrhoea. How is the child treated? And when is the child referred?
read.answer: The child is treated like any child coming in with the illness for the first time. The child is referred to a hospital for special care if the illness does not respond to the standard treatments, if the child becomes severely malnourished, or returns to the clinic repeatedly.

read.text: Case management can be effective only to the extent that families bring their sick children to a trained health worker for care in a timely way. If a family waits to bring a child to a clinic until the child is extremely sick or takes the child to an untrained provider, the child is more likely to die from the illness. Therefore, teaching families when to seek care is an important part of the case management process.
Check yourself
Why does effective case management need to consider all of a child's symptoms?
options: Because there are important relationships between the illnesses
Because each illness has its own separate guideline
Because the mother asks about only one problem
read.explanation: There are important relationships between the illnesses. For example, repeated diarrhoeal episodes often lead to malnutrition; diarrhoea, which often accompanies or follows measles, is particularly severe.

read.text: Why is teaching families when to seek care part of the case management process?
read.answer: Case management can be effective only to the extent that families bring their sick children to a trained health worker for care in a timely way. If a family waits until the child is extremely sick, or takes the child to an untrained provider, the child is more likely to die from the illness.

sections.title: The case management process

read.text: Name the six steps of the case management process and the charts that describe them.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: THE CASE MANAGEMENT PROCESS
The case management process is presented on a series of charts, which show the sequence of steps and provide information for performing them. The charts describe the following steps:

items: Assess the child or young infant.
Classify the illness.
Identify treatment.
Treat the child.
Counsel the mother.
Give follow-up care.

read.title: The six steps, one at a time

steps.title: Assess the child or young infant
steps.text: Taking a history and doing a physical examination.

steps.title: Classify the illness
steps.text: Making a decision on the severity of the illness: a category, or “classification”, for each of the child’s major symptoms.

steps.title: Identify treatment
steps.text: The charts recommend appropriate treatment for each classification.

steps.title: Treat the child
steps.text: Giving treatment in clinic, prescribing drugs or other treatments to be given at home, and also teaching the mother how to carry out the treatments.

steps.title: Counsel the mother
steps.text: Assessing how the child is fed and telling her about the foods and fluids to give the child and when to bring the child back to the clinic.

steps.title: Give follow-up care
steps.text: When the child comes back for a scheduled follow-up visit to check the child's improvement.

read.text: These steps are probably similar to the way you care for sick children now, though you may have learnt different words ton describe them. The step called “assess the child” means taking a history and doing a physical examination. “Classify the illness” means making a decision on the severity of the illness. You will select a category, or “classification” for each of the child’s major symptoms, which corresponds to the severity of the disease. Classifications are not specific disease diagnosis. Instead, they are categories that are used to determine treatment.

The charts recommend appropriate treatment for each classification. When using this process, selecting a classification on the chart is sufficient to allow you to identify treatment for a child. For example, a child with the classification VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE could have meningitis, severe malaria, or septicaemia. The treatments listed for VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE will be appropriate because they have been chosen to cover the most important diseases included in this classification.

“Treat” means giving treatment in clinic, prescribing drugs or other treatments to be given at home, and also teaching the mother how to carry out the treatments. “Counsel the mother” includes assessing how the child is fed and telling her about the foods and fluids to give the child and when to bring the child back to the clinic.
The case management process for sick children age 2 months up to 5 years is presented on three charts titled:

items: ASSESS AND CLASSIFY THE SICK CHILD
TREAT THE CHILD
COUNSEL THE MOTHER

read.text: Management of the young infant age up to 2 months is somewhat different from older infants and children. It is described on a different chart titled ASSESS, CLASSIFY, AND TREAT THE SDICK YOUNG INFANT.

The charts are designed to help health workers manage children correctly and efficiently. This course trains you to use the charts and gives you clinical practice managing sick children. After the course, the charts will help you recall and apply what you have learnt when managing sick children at your clinic.

read.title: Which chart?

cards.front: Sick child age 2 months up to 5 years
cards.back: ASSESS AND CLASSIFY THE SICK CHILD, TREAT THE CHILD, COUNSEL THE MOTHER

cards.front: Young infant age up to 2 months
cards.back: ASSESS, CLASSIFY, AND TREAT THE SICK YOUNG INFANT

read.text: Check yourself
A child is classified VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE. What does the classification tell you?
options: A category used to determine treatment, chosen to cover the most important diseases in it
That the child does not need treatment
read.explanation: Classifications are not specific disease diagnosis. They are categories that are used to determine treatment. A child with VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE could have meningitis, severe malaria, or septicaemia; the treatments listed cover the most important diseases.

sections.title: Purpose of this training course

read.text: Say who the course is for and list the skills you will learn.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: PURPOSE OF THIS TRAINING COURSE

This training course is designed to teach the case management process to doctors, nurses, and other health workers who see sick children and infants. It is a case management process for a first-level facility such as a clinic, a health center, or an outpatient department of a hospital. The course uses the word “clinic” throughout to mean any such setting.
You will learn to manage sick children according to the case management charts, including:

items: Assessing signs and symptoms of illness, and nutritional, immunization, and vitamin A supplementation status,
Classify the illness,
Identifying treatments for the child’s classifications and deciding if a child needs to be referred,

Giving important pre-referral treatments( such as a first dose of an antibiotic, vitamin A, quinine injection, diazepam given rectally, rapid acting bronchodilator and treatment to prevent low blood sugar) and referring the child,
Providing treatments in the clinic, such as oral rehydration therapy, vitamin A, and immunization,
Teaching the mother to give specific treatment at home, such as an oral antibiotic or antimalarial, oral salbutamol, and paracetamol,
Counseling the mother about feeding and when to return,
When a child comes for scheduled follow-up, reassess the problem and provide appropriate care.

read.text: Check yourself
Is it given before referral, in the clinic, or taught to the mother to give at home? Sort the treatments the way the book lists them.
groups: Taught to the mother for home

items.text: Treatment to prevent low blood sugar

read.explanation: These are the examples the book gives under each skill.

sections.title: Course methods and materials

read.text: Describe how you will learn in this course: modules, exercises, clinical sessions and your facilitator.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: COURSE METHODS AND MATERIALS
In addition to the case management charts, you will receive a series of booklets, called modules, which explain each step. They are titled::

items: 1. Assess and Classify the Sick Child Age 2 Months Up To 5 Years.
2. Identify Treatment.
3. Treat the Child.
4. Counsel the Mother.
5. Management of the Sick Young Infant Age Up To 2 Months.
6. Follow-up.

read.text: The modules include exercises that will help you learn the steps. Most exercises provide clinical information describing a sick child and ask questions. Some exercises use photographs or video. You will complete a module by reading it and working through the exercises. For approximately half of each day, you will go to nearby clinics to observe and practice managing sick children. In these clinical sessions you will assess, classify, and treat sick children, including teaching their mothers how to care for them at home.

The clinical sessions give you opportunities to try the skills that you learn about in the modules. You may ask questions and receive guidance if difficulties arise. By the end of the course, you will have experience managing children according to the case management process and can feel comfortable continuing at your own clinic.

A facilitator will guide you through the activities and exercises in the module, lead group discussions, and review your individual work on the modules. A facilitator will also supervise your practice during clinical sessions. You are encouraged to discuss any questions or problems with a facilitator.

A facilitator is a person who helps the participants learn the skills presented in the course. Your facilitator will: guide you through the course activities; answer questions as they arise, or find the answer if they do not know; clarify information you find confusing; give individual feedback on exercises where indicated; lead group discussions, drills, video exercises and role plays; prepare you for each clinical session and demonstrate tasks; and observe and help you as needed during your practice in outpatient sessions.
read.label: From your facilitator

read.text: Before you go on, think about your own work: what is the name of the clinic where you work, and what is your training or position? What is your responsibility for the care of sick children?
read.answer: Your facilitator asks every participant these questions at the start of the course. Keep your answers in mind: throughout the course you will be asked how you will use each skill in your own clinic.
read.label: Think about it

read.text: Check yourself
How will you complete a module?
options: By reading it and working through the exercises
read.explanation: You will complete a module by reading it and working through the exercises. Most exercises describe a sick child and ask questions; some use photographs or video.

sections.title: Selecting the right chart

read.text: Decide which age group a sick child is in, and select the right case management chart.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: The case management charts
read.caption: The narration is being recorded.

read.text: HOW TO SELECT THE APPROPRIATE CASE MANAGEMENT CHARTS?

Most clinics have a procedure for registering children and identifying whether they have come because they are sick, or for some other reason, such as for a well-child visit or an immunization session, or for care of an injury received in an accident. When a woman brings a child because the child is sick (due to illness, not trauma) and the child is sent to you for attention, you need to know the age of the child in order to select the appropriate chart and begin the assessment process. Depending on the procedure for registering patients at your clinic, the child’s name, age, and other information such as address may have been recorded already. If not, you may begin by asking the child’s name and age.
Decide which age group the child is in:

items: Age up to 2 months.
Age 2 months up to 5 years.

read.text: If the child is age 2 months up to 5 years, select the chart ASSESS AND CLASSIFY THE SICK CHILD AGE 2 MONTHS UP TO 5 YEARS. “Up to 5 years” means the child has not yet had his fifth birthday. For example, this age group includes a child who is 4 years 11 months but not a child who is 5 years old.
A child who is 2 months old would be in the group2 months up to 5 years, not in the group up to 2 months.
If the child is not yet 2 months of age, the child is considered a young infant. Use the chart ASSESS, CLASSIFY AND TREAT THE SICK YOUNG INFANT.

In the next module, Assess and Classify the Sick Child, you will learn how to assess and classify a child who is age 2 months up to 5 years. How to manage a young infant is taught later in the module Management of the Sick Young Infant.
“Up to” means up to but not including that age. “Up to 5 years” means the child has not yet had his fifth birthday.
read.label: From your facilitator

read.text: Which chart do you select? Sort each child.
groups: ASSESS AND CLASSIFY THE SICK CHILD AGE 2 MONTHS UP TO 5 YEARS
ASSESS, CLASSIFY AND TREAT THE SICK YOUNG INFANT

items.why: He has not yet had his fifth birthday.
A child who is 2 months old is in the group 2 months up to 5 years.
Not yet 2 months of age: a young infant.

items.text: A child who is 5 years old
items.why: “Up to 5 years” does not include a child who is 5 years old.

read.text: Why not use this process for children age 5 years or more?
read.answer: The case management process is designed for children less than 5 years of age. Although much of the advice on treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles and malnutrition is applicable to older children, the assessment and classification of older children would differ. For example, the cut-off rates for determining fast breathing would be different, because normal breathing rates are slower in older children. (From the facilitator guide.)
read.label: Discussion

read.text: Before you begin the next module, a reminder of what you will use: the case management process is described on charts. ASSESS AND CLASSIFY THE SICK CHILD, TREAT THE CHILD and COUNSEL THE MOTHER are used for sick children age 2 months up to 5 years. ASSESS, CLASSIFY AND TREAT THE SICK YOUNG INFANT is used from birth up to 2 months. You will learn all the steps from the modules and in clinical sessions. You are now ready to begin the first step of case management, assessing and classifying a sick child.
read.label: From your facilitator

sections.title: Glossary: Abscess to Holoendemic

read.text: Know where to find the meaning of a word used in the modules (Abscess to Holoendemic malaria area).
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Do not try to learn the glossary now. You will learn the terms in logical order as you study the modules. If you need help understanding a word when it is used in a module, look it up here, or ask a facilitator.
read.label: From your facilitator

read.text:
Abscess: a collection of pus.

Sterile abscess: an abscess that contains bacteria.

Abdomen: the area of the body containing the stomach and bowel.

Active feeding: encouraging a child to eat, for example, by sitting with him and helping to get the spoon into his mouth.

Active neurological disease of the nervous system: epilepsy and other current diseases of the brain or spinal cord. This does not include permanent, old neurological problems from cerebral palsy, polio, or injuries.

AIDS: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, caused by infection with the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). AIDS is the final and most severe phase of HIV infection. The immune system works poorly, and the patient may have various symptoms and diseases (such as diarrhoea, fever, wasting, pneumonia).

Amoebiasis: amoebic dysentery; dysentery caused by E. histolytica.

Allergies: problems such as sneezing, a rash, or difficult breathing that affect certain people when specific things are breathed in, eaten, injected, or touched.

Antidiarrhoeal drugs: drugs that are claimed to decrease or stop diarrhoea, such as antimotility drugs. These drugs are not useful for children with diarrhoea. Some are dangerous.

Antiemetics: drugs that control vomiting.

Antifolate drugs: drugs that act against folate. Both cotrimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole and the antimalarial sulfadoxine-pyramethamine (Fansidar) are antifolate drugs.

Antimotility drugs: drugs that slow the movement of contents through the bowel by reducing its muscular activity.

Appetite: the desire to eat.

Areola: the dark circle of skin around the nipple of the breast.

Aspiration: inhaling (breathing in) fluids.

Assess: to consider the relevant information and make a judgment. As used in this course, to examine the child and identify the signs of illness.

Axillary temperature: temperature measured in the armpit.

BCG: an immunization to prevent tuberculosis, given at birth. The initials stand for Bacille Calmette-Guerin.

Bowel: Intestine.

Breast cancer: malignant tumour that starts in the breast.

Breast milk substitute: Formula or milk given instead of or in addition to breast milk. An example is cow’s milk made as follows: mix half a cup (100ml) boiled whole cow’s milk with one quarter of a cup (50ml) of boiled water and 2 level teaspoons (10grams) of sugar.

Cerebral malaria: Falciparum malaria affecting the brain.

Checking questions: questions intended to find out what someone understands and what needs further explaining. After teaching a mother about feeding, a health worker might ask the checking question, “What foods will you feed your child?”

Chest indrawing: when the lower chest wall(lower ribs) goes in when a child breathes in. In a child age 2 months up to 5 years, if chest indrawing is clearly visible and present all the time during an examination, it is a sign of SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE.

Severe chest indrawing: chest indrawing that is very deep and easy to see. In a young infant, mild chest indrawing is normal, but severe chest indrawing is a sign of serious illness.

Chronic: lasting a long time or recurring frequently.

Classify: as used in this course, to select a category of illness and severity (called a classification) based on a child’s symptoms and signs.

Clinic: as used in this course, any first level outpatient health facility such as a dispensary, rural health post, health center, or the outpatient department of a hospital.

Communication skills: as used in this course, skills used in teaching and counseling with mothers, including: ASK AND LISTEN, PRAISE, ADVISE, AND CHECK UNDERSTANDING.

Complementary foods: foods given in addition to breast milk, starting when a child is 4-6 months of age. By age 6 months, all children should receive a nutritious, thick complementary food, such as cereal mixed with oil and bits of meat, vegetables, or fish. Complementary foods are sometimes called “weaning foods”.

Confidence: a feeling of being able to succeed.

Contraindication: a situation or condition in which a certain treatment, procedure, or drug should not be used.

Corneal rupture: bursting of the cornea, that is, the clear outer layer of the eye.

Counsel: as used in this module, to teach or advise a mother as part of the discussion which includes: asking questions, listening to the mother’s answers, praising and/or giving relevant advice, helping to solve problems, and checking understanding.

Counseling: the process of teaching or advising as described above.

Deficiency: a lack or shortage. Vitamin A deficiency is shortage of vitamin A in the body.

Dehydration: loss of a large amount of water and salts from the body.

Diagnostic test: special testing, such as laboratory tests or X rays, to determine the type or cause of illness.

Digest: to process food so it can be absorbed and used in the body.

Digital watch: a watch that shows the time in digits(numerals) instead of with moving hands.

Disease: as used in this course, a specific illness or group of illnesses, classified on the basis of signs and symptoms, for example, “VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE’. This classification includes several illnesses such as meningitis, cerebral malaria, and septicaemia.

DPT: immunization to prevent diphtheria, pertussis(whooping cough), and tetanus. For full protection a child needs 3 injections; at 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks.

Energy-rich: full of ingredients that that give energy(or calories), such as starches or oil.

Engorgement: a condition in which a mother’s breasts are swollen, hard, and painful because they are too full of milk.

Episodes: occurrence of a disease, Diarrhoeal episodes are occurrences of diarrhoea.

Essential: necessary. Essential vitamins and minerals (such as vitamins and iron) are those necessary for good health.

Essential fatty acids: fats that are necessary for a baby’s growing eyes and brain. These fatty acids are not present in cow’s milk or most brands of formula milk.

Exclusive breastfeeding: giving a child only breast milk and no additional food, water, or other fluids (with the exception of medicines and vitamins, if needed).

Expertise: a high level of skill in a particular area.

Falciparum malaria: malaria caused by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum.

Family foods: foods ordinarily eaten by the family

Febrile: having fever.

Feeding assessment: the process of asking questions to find out about a child’s usual feeding and feeding during illness. (Appropriate questions are listed on the COUNSEL chart).

Feeding bottle: a bottle with a nipple or teat that a child sucks on. Feeding bottles should not be used.

Feeding problems: differences between a child’s actual feeding and feeding recommendations listed on the COUNSEL chart, and other problems such as breast feeding, use of a feeding bottle, lack of active feeding, or not feeding well during illness.

Femoral artery: the main artery of the leg. Its pulsation can be felt in the groin (upper inner thigh).

Femoral vein: the main vein of the leg. It is located just medial to the femoral artery (that is, towards the middle of the body from the femoral artery).

Fever: as used in this course, fever includes: A history of fever Feeling hot to the touch An axillary temperature of 37.5ºC (99.5ºF) or higher, or a rectal temperature of 38ºC (100.4ºF) or higher.

First-level health facility: a facility such as a health center, clinic, rural health post, dispensary, or outpatient department of a hospital, which is considered the first facility within the health system where people seek care. In this course, the term clinic is used for any first-level health facility.

Folate: folic acid, a vitamin used in treatment of nutritional anaemia.

Follow-up visit: a return visit requested by the health worker to see if treatment is working or if further treatment or referral is needed.

Fontanelle: the soft spot on top of a young infant’s head, where the bones of the head have not come together.

Full-term: word used to describe a baby born after 37 weeks of pregnancy.

Glucose: a sugar used in oral rehydration salts and in IV fluids.

Gruel: a food made by boiling cereal meal or legumes in milk or water. Gruel may be made thick like porridge or thin like a drink. For complementary feeding, gruel should be made thick.

Grunting: soft, short sounds that a young infant makes when breathing out. Grunting occurs when a young infant is having trouble breathing.

Guilty: a feeling of having done wrong.

Haemoglobin: a protein containing iron that carries oxygen and makes the blood red.

Hepatitis B virus: one of the several viruses that causes hepatitis; this virus also causes liver cancer. This virus is spread easily by blood, so needles and syringes must be sterile.

HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus. HIV is the virus that causes AIDS.

Hookworm: a small worm that may live as a parasite in a person’s intestines and suck blood. This blood loss may lead to anaemia.

Holoendemic Malaria area: high-risk malaria area where transmission is throughout the year.

As used in this course, to select a category of illness and severity (called a classification) based on a child’s symptoms and signs.
As used in this course, any first level outpatient health facility such as a dispensary, rural health post, health center, or the outpatient department of a hospital.
As used in this course: a history of fever, feeling hot to the touch, or an axillary temperature of 37.5ºC (99.5ºF) or higher, or a rectal temperature of 38ºC (100.4ºF) or higher.

sections.title: Glossary: Hospital to Whipworm

read.text: Know where to find the meaning of a word used in the modules (Hospital to Whipworm).
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Do not try to learn the glossary now. You will learn the terms in logical order as you study the modules. If you need help understanding a word when it is used in a module, look it up here, or ask a facilitator.
read.label: From your facilitator

read.text:
Hospital: as used in this course, any health facility with inpatient beds, supplies, and expertise to treat a very sick child.

Hygienically: using clean utensils and clean hands, avoiding germs.

Hypernatraemia: too much sodium in the blood.

Hypothermia: low body temperature (below 35.5ºC Axillary or 36ºC rectal temperature).

Hypoxia: a condition in which too little oxygen is reaching the organs of the body.

Illness: sickness. As described in this course, 90the symptoms and signs of illness need to be assessed and classified in order to select treatment.

Immune suppression: weakening of the immune system so that the body has little resistance to disease.

Immune system: the system that helps the body resist disease by producing antibiotics or special cells to fight disease-causing agents.

Immunization status: a comparison of the child’s past immunizations with the recommended immunization schedule. Immunization status describes whether or not a child has received all of the immunizations recommended for his age, and, if not, what immunizations are needed now.

Incompetent: lacking the ability or skill to do something.

Infant: as used in this course, a baby up to 12 months.

Young infant: as used in this course, a baby age 1 week up to 2 months.

Infant feeding formulas: concentrated milk or soy products (to be combined with water) sold as a substitute for breast milk.

Initial visit: the first visit to a health worker for an episode of an illness or problem.

Inpatient: a patient who stays at a health facility and receives a bed and food as well as treatment.

Integrated: combined.

Integrated case management process: a process for treating patients that includes consideration of all of their symptoms.

Intramuscular (IM) injection: an injection (shot) put into a muscle, usually of the thigh.

Intravenous (IV) infusion: continuous slow introduction of a fluid into a vein.

Intravenous (IV) injection: an injection (shot) put directly into a vein.

Jaundiced: having a yellow colour in the eyes and skin.

Koplik spots: spots that occur in the mouth inside the cheek during the early stages of measles. They are small, irregular, bright red spots with a white spot in the center. They do not interfere with drinking or eating and do not need treatment.

Kwashiorkor: a type of protein-energy malnutrition due to lack of protein in the diet. A child with kwashiorkor has oedema, which may cause his limbs to appear puffy. The child may have sparse hair and dry scaly skin.

Lactulose: a sugar present in milk.

Local: present in the nearby geographic area. For example, local foods are those found in the area. (See “local infection” below for another meaning of local).

Local infections: infections located only in a specific place on the body, for example, in the eye or in the mouth.

Low blood sugar: too little sugar in the blood, also called hypoglycemia.

Low birthweight: low weight at birth, due either to poor growth in the womb or to prematurity (being born early). Children less than 2500 grams have low birthweight.

Malignant: tending to spread and result in death.

Marasmus: a type of protein-energy malnutrition due to long-term lack of calories and protein. A child with marasmus appears to be just like “skin and bones”.

Mastoid: the skull bone behind the ear.

Measles complications: problems or infections that occur during or after measles. Some examples of measles complications are diarrhoea, pneumonia, stridor, mouth ulcers, ear infection, and eye infection. A less common complication is encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain.

Meningitis: a dangerous infection in which the spinal cord and the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal column become infected.

Midwife: a health care worker who assists women in childbirth and may also provide other health care.

Main symptoms: as used in this course, those symptoms which the health worker should ask the mother about when assessing the child. The four main symptoms listed on the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY chart are: cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, and ear problem.

Nasogastric (NG) tube: a tube inserted through a patient’s nose to his stomach. An NG tube may be used to give ORS solution to severely dehydrated patients when IV therapy is not available, or to feed a severely malnourished child who cannot eat.

Nutrient: a substance in food that helps one grow and be healthy, such as protein, minerals, and vitamins.

Nutrient-rich: full of the essential nutrients. These include proteins as well as vitamins and minerals.

Nutritional status: the degree to which a child shows or does not show certain signs of malnutrition or anaemia or low weight. In this course, a child’s nutritional status may be classified as: SEVERE MALNUTRITION OR SEVERE ANAEMIA, ANAEMIA OR VERY LOW WEIGHT, or NO ANAEMIA AND NOT VERY LOW WEIGHT.

Oedema: swelling from excess fluid under the skin. Oedema usually occurs in the lower legs and feet, sometimes elsewhere.

Oppoprtunistic infection: infections caused by microorganisms, which the body’s immune system is normally able to fight off. When the immune system is weakened, as in AIDS, opportunistic infections can take hold. For example, in a healthy person, there are organisms in the mouth, which do not normally cause infection; however, in a person with a weakened immune system, these same organisms may cause oral thrush.

Outreach service (activity): vaccination activities conducted in villages or vaccination sites, which are not within easy walking distance of the health center.

Outreach team, mobile team: is a group of health workers who travel from the health center to a village or vaccination site to conduct outreach vaccination sessions and return to the health center in the same day.

Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS): a mixture of glucose and salt conforming to the WHO recommended formula (in grams per liter): sodium chloride 3.5; trisodium citrate dehydrate 2.9, or sodium bicarbonate 2.5; potassium chloride 1.5; and glucose 20.0.

OPV: oral polio vaccine. To prevent polio, it is given in 4 doses: at birth, 6weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks.

Outpatient: a patient who does not stay overnight at a health facility.

Ovarian cancer: malignant tumour starting in the ovary (the female sex glands in which eggs are formed).

Overwhelmed: feeling as though there is too much to be remembered.

Parasite: an organism living in or on another organism and causing it harm.

Pathogen: an organism or microorganism that causes disease.

Persist: to remain or endure.

Practical: possible to do with the time and resources available.

Pre-referral: before referral to a hospital.

Premature: born early, before 37 weeks of pregnancy.

Protein: a substance in food made up of amino acids needed for adequate growth. Meat, fish, eggs, milk, and beans are examples of foods containing protein.

Protein-energy malnutrition: a condition caused by lack of enough protein or energy in the diet, or by frequent illness.

Pulses: legumes, such as peas, beans, or lentils.

Pustule: a reddish bump on the skin containing pus.

Radial pulse: the pulse felt over the radial artery, which is the main blood vessel at the wrist on the outside of the thumb.

Reassessment: as used in this course, to examine the child again for signs of specific illness to see if the child is improving.

Full reassessment: to do the entire assessment process on the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY chart again to see if there has been improvement and also to assess and classify any new problems.

Recommendations: advice, instructions that should be followed.

Recurrent convulsions: spasms or fits that occur repeatedly.

Reduce, reduction: decrease.

Referral: as used in this course, sending a patient for further assessment and care at a hospital.

Relactation: starting breastfeeding again and producing breast milk after stopping.

Respiratory distress: discomfort from not getting enough air into the lungs.

Semi-solid food: food that is part solid and part liquid. A soft wet food such as gruel or porridge is semi-solid.

Septicemia: an infection of the blood, also called sepsis in this course.

Severe classification: as used in this course, a very serious illness requiring urgent attention and usually referral or admissions for inpatient care. Severe classifications are listed in pink-coloured rows on the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY CHART.

Shock: a dangerous condition with severe weakness, lethargy, or unconsciousness, cold extremities, and fast, weak pulse. It is caused by diarrhoea with very severe dehydration, hemorrhage, burns, or sepsis.

Signs: as used in this course, physical evidence of a health problem, which the health worker observes by looking, listening, or feeling. Examples of signs include: fast breathing, chest indrawing, sunken eyes, stiff neck, pus draining from the ear…etc.

Stable: staying the same rather than getting worse.

Stridor: a harsh musical voice heard during inspiration.

Symptoms: as used in this course, health problems reported by the mother such as cough, diarrhoea, or ear pain.

Thrush: ulcers or white patches on the inside of the mouth and tongue caused by a yeast infection.

Trophozoites: stage of a protozoan organism such as Giardia lamblia or E. histolytica; the stage that causes tissue damage.

Ulcer: a painful open sore. Mouth ulcers are sores on the inside of the mouth and lips or on the tongue. These may occur with measles and may be red or have white coating on them. They make it difficult to eat or drink.

Upright: vertical (standing up).

Semi-upright: partly upright, leaning.

Urgent: requiring immediate attention, important to save a child’s life.

Urgent referral: sending a patient immediately for further care at a hospital.

Uterus: womb.

Vulnerable: endangered, likely to become ill.

Weaning foods: another term for complementary foods, given in addition to breastmilk starting at 4-6 months of age.

Wheezing: a soft musical voice heard during expiration.

Whipworm: a small worm that may live as a parasite in a person’s intestine and suck blood. This blood loss may lead to anaemia and diarrhoea.

cards.back: The four main symptoms listed on the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY chart are: cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, and ear problem.
Physical evidence of a health problem, which the health worker observes by looking, listening, or feeling.
Health problems reported by the mother such as cough, diarrhoea, or ear pain.
A very serious illness requiring urgent attention and usually referral or admissions for inpatient care. Listed in pink-coloured rows on the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY CHART.

modules.title: Module 2: Assess and classify the sick child age 2 months up to 5 years

sections.title: Introduction to assess and classify

read.text: Say what the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY chart helps you do, and list what you will learn in this module.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Assess and classify: an overview
read.caption: The narration is being recorded.

read.text: INTRODUCTION

A mother brings her sick child to the clinic for a particular problem or symptom. If you only assess the child for that particular problem or symptom, you might overlook other signs of disease. The child might have pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, measles, or malnutrition. These diseases can cause death or disability in young children if they are not treated. The chart ASSESS AND CLASSIFY THE SICK CHILD AGE 2 MONTHS UP TO 5 YEARS describes how to assess and classify sick children so that signs of disease are not overlooked. According to the chart, you should ask the mother about the child's problem and check the child for general danger signs. Then ask about the four main symptoms: cough or difficult breathing, diarrhea, fever and ear problem. A child who has one or more of the main symptoms could have a serious illness. When a main symptom is present, ask additional questions to help classify the illness. Check the child for malnutrition and Anemia. Also, check the child's immunization and vitamin A supplementation status and assess other problems the mother has mentioned.
LEARNING OBJECTIVES:
This module will describe and allow you to practice the following skills:

• Asking the mother about child's problem.
  • Checking for general danger signs.
  • Asking the mother about the four main symptoms:
    • Cough or difficult breathing
    • Diarrhea
    • Fever
    • Ear problem.
  • When a main symptom is present:
    • Assessing the child further for signs related to the main symptom
    • Classifying the illness according to the signs, which are present, or absent.
  • Checking for signs of malnutrition and anemia and classifying the child's nutritional status and ANWMIA.
  • Checking the child's immunization and vitamin A supplementation status and deciding if the child needs any immunizations or vitamin A supplementation.
  • Assessing any other problems.
  • Assessing mother’s health needs
Your facilitator will tell you more about the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart.

The ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart has three columns: Assess, Classify as, and Identify treatment. In this module you use the first two. Keep your chart booklet open beside you: from now on you will look at the chart at every step.
read.label: From your facilitator

read.text: Check yourself
Which four main symptoms do you ask about for every sick child?
options: Cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever and ear problem
read.explanation: Ask about the four main symptoms: cough or difficult breathing, diarrhea, fever and ear problem.

sections.title: Ask the mother what the child's problems are

read.text: Greet the mother, find the child's age, ask about the problems with good communication, and decide if this is an initial or follow-up visit.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 1.0 ASK THE MOTHER WHAT THE CHILD’S PROBLEMS ARE

A mother (or other family member such as the father, grandmother, sister or brother) usually brings a child to the clinic because the child is sick. But mothers also bring children for well-child visits, immunization sessions and for treatment of injuries. The steps on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart describe what you should do when a mother brings her child to the clinic because he is sick. The chart should not be used for a well-child brought for immunization or for a child with an injury or burn.
When should the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart be used?
options: When a mother brings her child because he is sick
For a well-child brought for immunization
For a child with an injury or a burn
read.explanation: The steps on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart describe what you should do when a mother brings her child to the clinic because he is sick. The chart should not be used for a well-child brought for immunization or for a child with an injury or burn.

read.text: When patients arrive at most clinics, the clinic staffs identify the reason for the child's visit. Clinic staffs obtain the child's weight height ,or length and temperature and record them on a patient chart, another written record, or on a small piece of paper. Then the mother and child see a health worker.
When you see the mother and her sick child:

items: Greet the mother appropriately and ask her to sit with her child.
You need to know the child's age so you can choose the right case management chart; Look at the child's record to find the child's age.
If the child age is 2 months up to 5 years, assess and classify the child according to the steps on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart.

If the child from birth up to 2 months, assess and classify the young infant according to the steps on the YOUNG INFANT chart. (You will learn more about managing sick young infants later in the course.)

Look to see if the child's weight, length or height, mid- upper arm circumference (MUAC) and temperature have been measured and recorded. If not, weigh the child and measure his length or height, (MUAC) and temperature later when you assess and classify the child's main symptoms. Do not undress or disturb the child now.
Ask the mother about the child's problems.

read.text: Record what the mother tells you about the child's problems; An important reason for asking this question is to open good communication with the mother. Using of good communication helps to reassure the mother that her child will receive good care. When you treat the child's illness later in the visit, you will need to teach and advise the mother about caring for her sick child at home. So, it is important to have good communication with the mother from the beginning of the visit.
Why is it important to have good communication with the mother from the beginning of the visit?
read.answer: Using good communication helps to reassure the mother that her child will receive good care. When you treat the child's illness later in the visit, you will need to teach and advise the mother about caring for her sick child at home.

read.text:
• Use Good Communication skills:
    • Listen carefully to what the mother tells you. This will show her that you are taking her concerns seriously.
    • Use words the mother understands. If she does not understand the questions you asked her, she cannot give the information you need to assess and classify the child correctly.
    • Give the mother time to answer the questions. For example, she may need time to decide if the sign you asked about is present.
    • Ask additional questions when the mother is not sure about her answer. When you ask about a main symptom or related sign, the mother may not be sure if it is present. Ask her additional questions to help her give clear answers.
  • Determine if this is an initial or follow-up visit for this problem.
    • If this is the child's first visit for this episode of an illness or problem, then this is an initial visit.
    • If the child was seen a few days ago for the same illness, this is a follow- up visit.

A follow-up visit has a different purpose than an initial visit. During a follow-up visit, the health worker finds out if the treatment he gave during the initial visit has helped the child. If the child is not improving or is getting worse after a few days, the health worker refers the child to a hospital or changes the child's treatment.
What does the health worker find out during a follow-up visit?
options: Whether the treatment given at the initial visit has helped the child
read.explanation: During a follow-up visit, the health worker finds out if the treatment he gave during the initial visit has helped the child. If the child is not improving or is getting worse after a few days, the health worker refers the child to a hospital or changes the child's treatment.

read.text: How you find out if this is an initial or follow-up visit depends on how your clinic registers patients and identifies the reason for their visit. Some clinics give mothers follow-up slips that tell them when to return. In other clinics, the health worker writes a follow-up note on the multi-visit card or chart. Or, when the patient registers, clinic staffs ask the mother questions to find out why she has come.
You will learn how to carry out a follow-up visit later in the course. The examples and exercises in this module describe children who have come for an initial visit.
Initial visit or follow-up visit?

items.text: This is the child's first visit for this episode of an illness or problem.
The child was seen a few days ago for the same illness.
The health worker finds out if the treatment given at the first visit has helped the child.

read.text: Check yourself
Why is it important to ask the mother about the child's problems?
options: To open good communication with the mother
To decide the dose of antibiotic
read.explanation: An important reason for asking this question is to open good communication with the mother.

read.text: A mother brings her child for immunization. He is well. Do you use the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart?
options: No, the chart should not be used for a well child brought for immunization
read.explanation: The chart should not be used for a well-child brought for immunization or for a child with an injury or burn.

sections.title: Check for general danger signs

read.text: Ask and look for the five general danger signs, and know what to do when a child has one.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: A child sleeps on her mother's lap. Is she lethargic?
options: Not necessarily: wake her and look
No, sleeping children are never sick
feedback: Sleeping is not the same as lethargic.
Right. Look at how she wakes and responds.
A sleeping child can be lethargic. You must look.

read.text: 2.0 ASK AND CHECK FOR GENERAL DANGER SIGNS
Check ALL sick children for general danger signs.
A general danger sign is present if:

items: The child is not able to drink or breastfeed
The child vomits everything
The child has had convulsions
The child is lethargic or unconscious.
The child is convulsing now

read.text: A child with a general danger sign has a serious problem. Most children with a general danger sign need URGENT referral to hospital. They may need lifesaving treatment with injectable antibiotics, oxygen or other treatments, which may not be available in your clinic. Complete the rest of the assessment immediately. How to provide urgent treatment is described in the module Identify Treatment.
Here is the first box in the "Assess" column. It tells you how to check for general danger signs.

ASK THE MOTHER WHAT THE CHILD’S PROBLEMS ARE
   • Determine if this is an initial or follow-up visit for this problem.
      o If follow-up visit, use the follow-up instructions on TREAT THE CHILD chart.
      o If initial visit, assess the child as follows:

        ASK AND CHECK FOR GENERAL DANGER SIGNS

        ASK AND CHECK:                                              LOOK:
        Is the child not able to drink or breastfeed?            If the child is lethargic or unconscious.
        Does the child vomit everything?                          If the child is convulsing now.
        Has the child had convulsions?

             A child with any general danger sign needs URGENT attention; complete the Assessment and
 give any pre-referral treatment immediately so referral is not delayed.
             If the child is convulsing now, manage the airway and treat the child with DIAZEPAM. Then
 rapidly assess, classify and provide other treatment before referring to hospital.

read.caption: The same box in your chart booklet (Sudan national protocol).

read.text: Name the five general danger signs.
read.answer: Not able to drink or breastfeed; vomits everything; has had convulsions; lethargic or unconscious; convulsing now.

sections.title: Ask and look for each general danger sign

read.text: Decide if a child is not able to drink, vomits everything, has had convulsions, is lethargic or unconscious, or is convulsing now.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Checking for general danger signs
read.caption: The narration is being recorded.

read.title: Exercise: identifying lethargic or unconscious (part 1 of 2)
Exercise: identifying lethargic or unconscious (part 2 of 2)

read.text: When you check for general danger signs:
ASK: Is the child able to drink or breastfeed?
A child has the sign "not able to drink or breastfeed" if the child is too weak to drink and is not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink or breast milk.
A breastfed child cannot suck because his nose is blocked. You clear the nose and he can then breastfeed. Does he have the danger sign?
options: Yes: not able to drink or breastfeed
No: the nose was blocked, and he can breastfeed once it is cleared
read.explanation: A child who is breastfed may have difficulty sucking when his nose is blocked. If the child can breastfeed after his nose is cleared, the child does not have the danger sign, "not able to drink or breastfeed."

read.text: When you ask the mother if the child is able to drink, make sure that she understands the question. If she says that the child is not able to drink or breastfeed, ask her to offer the child a drink of clean water or breast milk. Look to see if the child is swallowing the water or breast milk.

A child who is breastfed may have difficulty sucking when his nose is blocked. If the child's nose is blocked, clear it. If the child can breastfeed after his nose is cleared, the child does not have the danger sign, "not able to drink or breastfeed."
ASK: Does the child vomit everything?

A child who is not able to hold anything in stomach at all has the sign "vomits everything." What goes down comes back up, a child who vomits several times but can hold down some fluids does not have this general danger sign. When you ask the question, use words the mother understands. Give her time to answer.
A child vomits several times but holds down some fluids. Does he have the danger sign "vomits everything"?
read.explanation: A child who vomits several times but can hold down some fluids does not have this general danger sign.

read.text: If the mother is not sure if the child is vomiting everything, help her to make her answer clear. For example, ask the mother how often the child vomits. Also, ask if each time the child swallows’ food or fluids, does the child vomit? If you are not sure of the mother's answers, ask her to offer the child a drink. See if the child vomits.
ASK: Has the child had convulsions?
During a convulsion, the child's arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child may lose consciousness or not be able to respond to spoken directions.

Convulsions may be the result of fever. In this instance, they do little harm beyond frightening the mother. But convulsions may be associated with meningitis, cerebral malaria or other life-threatening conditions.
Name two words a mother may use for convulsions, and say why you use words she understands.
read.answer: The mother may know convulsions as "fits" or "spasms." Use words the mother understands.

read.text: Ask the mother if the child has had convulsions during this current illness. Use words the mother understands. For example, the mother may know convulsions as "fits" or "spasms."
LOOK: See if the child is lethargic or unconscious.

A lethargic child is not awake and alert when he should be. He is drowsy and does not show interest in what is happening around him. Often the lethargic child does not look at his mother or watch your face when you talk. The child may stare blankly and appear not to notice what is going on around him.
An unconscious child cannot be wakened. He does not respond when he is touched, shaken or spoken to.
A sleeping child wakens when the mother talks to him or you clap your hands. Is he lethargic or unconscious?
options: Neither: he was asleep, which is not abnormal
read.explanation: If the child wakens, it means the child was asleep. This is not abnormal.

read.text: Ask the mother if the child seems unusually sleepy or if she cannot wake the child. Look to see if the child wakens when the mother talks or shakes the child or when you clap your hands. If the child wakens, it means the child was asleep. This is not abnormal.
Note: If the child is sleeping and has cough or difficult breathing, count the number of breaths first before you try to wake the child.
LOOK: See if the child is convulsing now:
During a convulsion, the child’s arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child loses consciousness or is not able to respond to spoken directions.

If the child is convulsing in the clinic now, treat the child by managing the airway and giving diazepam. How to manage the airway and how to give diazepam are described in the module treat the child.
If the child has a general danger sign refer UREGENTY to hospital, complete the rest of assessment immediately. this child has a severe problem. there must be no delay in his prerefral treatment.
Check yourself
A child vomits several times, but can hold down some fluids. Does he have the general danger sign “vomits everything”?
read.explanation: A child who vomits several times but can hold down some fluids does not have this general danger sign.

read.text: A breastfed child cannot suck. His nose is blocked. After you clear the nose he breastfeeds well. Is he “not able to drink or breastfeed”?
read.explanation: If the child can breastfeed after his nose is cleared, the child does not have the danger sign, "not able to drink or breastfeed."

read.text: A sleeping child has cough. What do you do first?
options: Wake him to look for lethargy
Count the number of breaths first
read.explanation: If the child is sleeping and has cough or difficult breathing, count the number of breaths first before you try to wake the child.

read.text: A child has a general danger sign. What must you do?
read.answer: Refer URGENTLY to hospital and complete the rest of the assessment immediately. This child has a severe problem: there must be no delay in his pre-referral treatment.

sections.title: Practise: general danger signs

read.text: Find the general danger signs in three children, and in a conversation with a mother.
read.label: In this lesson
Conversation
read.title: Ask about the danger signs

dialogue.text: Good morning. What is the problem with your son today?
He has had a cough and fever for three days.
Is he able to drink or breastfeed?
Yes, he breastfeeds, but less than usual.

stages.question: What do you ask next?
options: How many children do you have?
stages.explanation: Ask about each general danger sign in turn before anything else.
feedback: Right. Ask about each danger sign, one at a time.
Immunization is checked later, after assess and classify.
This is not part of checking for danger signs.

dialogue.text: No, he keeps the milk down.
Has he had convulsions during this illness?
Yes, yesterday evening he shook all over for a short time.

stages.question: What does this mean?
options: He has a general danger sign
It is only from the fever, so it does not count
stages.explanation: Convulsions during this illness are a general danger sign: the child needs urgent attention.
feedback: Right.
Convulsions in this illness count whatever the cause.
A child with a danger sign must not wait.

read.label: Test your skill
read.title: Does the child have a general danger sign?

cases.text: Huda's mother says Huda has vomited since this morning. When you ask, she says Huda vomits everything she eats or drinks, even water. Huda is awake and looks at you. She has had no convulsions.

record.title: Check for general danger signs
lines: Not able to drink or breastfeed: no

cases.question: Does Huda have a general danger sign?
options: No: she is awake and alert
Not sure until you count her breaths
feedback: Right. A child who cannot keep anything down vomits everything. This is a general danger sign.
Being awake does not rule out a danger sign. Huda vomits everything, even water.
Breathing is part of the cough assessment. The danger signs are checked first, and Huda already has one.
cases.explanation: A child with any general danger sign needs URGENT attention: complete the assessment and any pre-referral treatment immediately, then refer.

cases.text: Adam has had fever for 2 days. His father says that last night Adam's arms and legs jerked and he did not respond for a few minutes. Now Adam is drinking and looks at you.

record.title: Check for general danger signs

cases.question: Adam is drinking and alert now. Does he have a general danger sign?
options: No, because he is alert now
Only if he convulses in the clinic
feedback: A convulsion during this illness is a general danger sign even if the child looks well now.

The front of the Recording Form is similar to the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart. It lists questions to ask the mother and the signs, for which you should look, listen and feel. In most of the exercises in this module, you will only use part of the Recording Form. As you learn each step in the chart, you will use more of it.
Your facilitator will show you a Recording Form and tell you how to use

This is a Recording Form. There are 2 sides: the front side is similar to the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart; the other side is used to plan the child's treatment, later in the course. At the top you write the child's name, age, weight, height or length, MUAC and temperature, the mother's answer about the child's problems, and whether this is an initial or follow-up visit. The form has two columns, Assess and Classify, like the chart. You record by circling any sign that is present, ticking Yes or No after each main symptom, writing numbers such as the breaths per minute or the number of days, and writing the classification in the Classify column. The reminder “Remember to use danger sign when selecting classifications” tells you to consider the general danger sign when you classify each main symptom. sections.title: Assess cough or difficult breathing: how long, and count the breaths

read.text: Ask about cough or difficult breathing and its duration, count the breaths in one minute and decide if there is fast breathing.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: A child of 8 months breathes 48 times a minute. Is that fast?
options: It depends on the child's age
feedback: 48 is below the cut-off for 8 months (50).
Right for 8 months, but think about why.
Right. The cut-off is 50 from 2 up to 12 months and 40 from 12 months up to 5 years. At 8 months 48 is not fast.

read.text: 3.0 ASSESS and classify COUGH OR DIFFICULT BREATHING
3.1 ASSESS COUGH OR DIFFICULT BREATHING
A child with cough or difficult breathing is assessed for:

items: How long the child has had cough or difficult breathing?
Fast breathing
Chest indrawing
Stridor in a calm child
Wheezing Here is the box in the "Assess" column that lists the steps for assessing a child for cough or difficult breathing:

read.text:
THEN ASK ABOUT MAIN SYMPTOMS
Does the child have cough or difficult breathing?
    IF YES, ASK:                                LOOK, LISTEN,
     For how long?                         - Count the breaths in one-minute        CHILD MUST
                                            - Look for chest indrawing.              BE CALM
                                            - Look and listen for stridor.
                                            - Look and listen for wheeze

read.caption: The same box in your chart booklet.

read.text: For ALL sick children, ask about cough or difficult breathing.
ASK: Does the child have cough or difficult breathing?
"Difficult breathing" is any unusual pattern of breathing. Mothers describe this in different ways. They may say that their child's breathing is "fast", "noisy", or "interrupted."
A child has had a cough for more than 2 weeks. What does the book say this may be a sign of?
options: Tuberculosis, asthma, whooping cough or another problem
read.explanation: A child who has a cough or difficulty breathing for more than 2 weeks has a chronic cough. This may be a sign of tuberculosis, asthma, whooping cough or another problem.

read.text: If the mother answers NO, look to see if you think the child has cough or difficult breathing. If the child does not have cough or difficult breathing, ask about the next main symptom, diarrhea. Do not assess the child further for signs related to cough or difficult breathing.
If the mother answers YES, or you think the child has cough or difficult breathing, and then ask the next question.
ASK: For how long?
A child who has a cough or difficulty breathing for more than 2 weeks has a chronic cough. This may be a sign of tuberculosis, asthma, whooping cough or another problem
COUNT the breaths in one minute:

• You must count the breaths the child takes in one minute to decide if the child has fast breathing. The child must be quiet and calm when you look and listen to his breathing. If the child is frightened, crying or angry, you will not be able to obtain an accurate count of the child's breaths.
  • Tell the mother you are going to count her child's breathing. Remind her to keep her child calm. If the child is sleeping, do not wake the child.
  • To count the number of breaths in one minute, there are a number of methods you can use:
  • 1. Use a watch with a second hand or a digital watch
    • i. Sounding timer that sounds offer one minute (60 seconds). Count the child’s breaths for one minute.
    • ii. Use a watch with a second hand or a digital watch, or ask another health worker to watch the second hand and tell you when 60 seconds have passed. You look at the child's chest and count the number of breaths.
    • iii. If you cannot find another health worker to help you, put the watch where you can see the second hand. Glance at the second and as you count the breaths, the child takes in one minute.
  • 2. Look for breathing movement anywhere on the child's chest or abdomen usually you can see breathing movements even on a child who is dressed. If you cannot see this movement easily, ask the mother to lift the child's shirt. If the child starts to cry, ask the mother to calm the child before you start counting.

If you are not sure about the number of breaths you counted (for example, if the child was actively moving and it was difficult to watch the chest, or if the child was upset or crying), repeat the count.

read.title: Fast breathing: the cut-off by age

cards.front: A child who is exactly 12 months old
cards.back: Fast breathing if you count 40 breaths per minute or more

read.text: The cut-off for fast breathing depends on the child's age. Normal breathing rates are higher in children age 2 months up to 12 months than in children age 12 months up to 5 years.

If the child is:                                   The child has fast breathing if you count:

2 months up to 12 months                           50 breaths per minute or more

12 months up to 5 years                            40breaths per minute or more

Note: The child who is exactly 12 months old has fast breathing if you count 40 breaths per minute or more. Before you look for the next three signs -- chest indrawing, stridor, and wheeze --watch the child to determine when the child is breathing IN and when the child is breathing OUT.

2 months up to 12 months: 50 or more.

items.text: Exactly 12 months old, 44 breaths per minute
items.why: The child who is exactly 12 months old has fast breathing if you count 40 or more.
12 months up to 5 years: 40 or more.
12 months up to 5 years: 40 or more.

read.text: You are not sure about the number of breaths you counted: the child was moving and crying. What do you do?
read.answer: Repeat the count. The child must be quiet and calm when you look and listen to his breathing.

sections.title: Look for chest indrawing, stridor and wheeze

read.text: Recognise chest indrawing, stridor in a calm child, and wheeze.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: LOOK for chest indrawing.
You see the lower chest wall go IN only when the child is crying. Does he have chest indrawing?
options: No: it must be clearly visible and present all the time
read.explanation: For chest indrawing to be present, it must be clearly visible and present all the time. If you only see chest indrawing when the child is crying or feeding, the child does not have chest indrawing.

items: If you did not lift the child's shirt when you counted the child's breaths, ask the mother to lift it now.

Look for chest indrawing when the child breathes IN. Look at the lower chest wall (lower ribs). The child has chest indrawing if the lower chest wall goes IN when the child breathes IN. Chest indrawing occurs when the effort the child needs to breathe in is much greater than normal. In normal breathing, the whole chest wall (upper and lower) and the abdomen move OUT when the child breathes IN. When chest indrawing is present, the lower chest wall goes IN when the child breathes IN.

If you are not sure that chest indrawing is present, look again. If the child's body is bent at the waist, it is hard to see the lower chest wall move. Ask the mother to change the child's position so he is lying flat in her lap. If you still do not see the lower chest wall go IN when the child breathes IN, the child does not have chest indrawing.
For chest indrawing to be present, it must be clearly visible and present all the time. If you only see chest indrawing when the child is crying or feeding, the child does not have chest indrawing.

If only the soft tissue between the ribs goes in when the child breathes in (also called intercostal indrawing or intercostal retractions), the child does not have chest indrawing. In this assessment, chest indrawing is lower chest wall indrawing.11 It does not include "intercostal indrawing." This is the same as "subcostal indrawing" or "subcostal retractions."

read.text: LOOK and LISTEN for Stridor:
When do you look and listen for stridor, and why?
read.answer: Be sure to look and listen for stridor when the child is calm. A child who is not very ill may have stridor only when he is crying or upset. A child who has stridor when calm has a dangerous condition.

items: Stridor is a harsh noise made when the child breathes IN. Stridor happens when there is a swelling of the larynx, trachea or epiglottis. This swelling interferes with air entering the lungs. It can be life threatening when the swelling causes the child's airway to be blocked. A child who has stridor when calm has a dangerous condition.
Look to see when the child breathes IN. Then listen for stridor. Put your ear near the child's mouth because stridor can be difficult to hear.

Sometimes you will hear a wet noise if the nose is blocked. Clear the nose, and listen again. A child who is not very ill may have stridor only when he is crying or upset. Be sure to look and listen for stridor when the child is calm.

read.text: LOOK and LISTEN for Wheeze:

items: A child with wheezing makes a soft musical noise or shows signs that breathing OUT is difficult.
Look to see when the child is breathing OUT. Listen for the wheeze noise by holding your ear near the child’s mouth, since the noise may be difficult to hear.
Wheezing is caused by a narrowing of the air passages in the lungs when the child breathes out. The breathing out takes longer than normal and requires effort.
Sometimes so little air moves that there is no noise. Look to see if the breathing out phase requires great effort, and is longer than normal

If the child is wheezing, ask the mother if her child has had a previous episode of wheezing within the last year. A child with “recurrent wheeze” has had more than one episode of wheeze in a 12-month period.

read.caption: Chest indrawing: the lower chest wall goes IN when the child breathes IN.

read.text: Check yourself
The soft tissue between the ribs goes in when the child breathes in. The lower chest wall does not. Is there chest indrawing?
read.explanation: If only the soft tissue between the ribs goes in (intercostal indrawing), the child does not have chest indrawing.

read.text: You see chest indrawing only when the child is crying. Is chest indrawing present?
read.explanation: For chest indrawing to be present, it must be clearly visible and present all the time.

read.text: Stridor or wheeze?

items.text: A harsh noise when the child breathes IN
A soft musical noise when the child breathes OUT
Caused by swelling of the larynx, trachea or epiglottis
Caused by narrowing of the air passages in the lungs

sections.title: Classification tables

read.text: Read a classification table: what the pink, yellow and green rows mean, and how to select one row.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 3.2 CLASSIFY COUGH OR DIFFICULT BREATHING CLASSIFICATION TABLES:

Signs of illness and their classifications are listed on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart in classification tables. Most classification tables have three rows. If the chart is in color, each row is colored pink, yellow, or green. The color of the rows tells you quickly if the child has a serious illness. You can also quickly choose the appropriate treatment.

items: A classification in the pink row needs urgent attention and referral or admission for inpatient care. This is a severe classification.

A classification in a yellow row means that the child needs an appropriate antibiotic, an oral antimalarial or other treatment. The treatment includes teaching the mother how to give the oral drugs or to treat local infections at home. The health worker advises her about caring for the child at home and when she should return.

A classification in a green row means the child does not need treatment with antibiotics. The health worker teaches the mother how to care for her child at home. For example, you might advise her on feeding her sick child or giving fluid for diarrhea.

read.text: Depending on the combination of the child's signs and symptoms, the child is classified in the pink, yellow, or the green row. That is, the child is classified only once in each classification table.

Most classification tables on the chart have 3 rows, coloured pink, yellow or green. Always start at the top (pink) row. If the child does not have a severe classification, look at the yellow (middle) row. If the child has no sign in the yellow row, go to the green (bottom) row. If the child has signs from more than one row, always select the more serious classification.

items.text: Needs urgent attention and referral or admission for inpatient care

read.text: A child has a sign in the pink row and a sign in the yellow row. Which classification do you select?
options: The more serious classification, in the pink row
read.explanation: The child is classified only once in each classification table. Select the more serious classification.

sections.title: Classify cough or difficult breathing

read.text: Select SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE, PNEUMONIA, or COUGH OR COLD.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: There are three possible classifications for a child with cough or difficult breathing. They are:

items: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE or
PNEUMONIA or
COUGH OR COLD

read.text: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE

A child with any general danger sign or stridor when calm is classified as having SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE PNEUMONIA A child with a cough or difficulty breathing who has chest indrawing or fast breathing and NOgeneral danger signs and NO stridor when calm is classified as having PNEUMONIA If the child is wheezing and does NOT a general danger sign or stridor, test the child for pneumonia by giving rapid acting bronchodilator. Watch the relevant video in the SEE part of this Training unit for how to give a rapid acting bronchodilator. Wait for 20 minutes and reassess the child. If there is, still chest indrawing or fast breathing, repeat the test twice before classifying the child’s illness as pneumonia. COUGH OR COLD A child with cough or difficult breathing who has no general danger signs, no stridor when calm, no chest indrawing, and no fast breathing is classified as having COUGH OR COLD.

cells: Any general danger sign or Stridor in calm child
SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
No signs of pneumonia or very severe disease

cards.label: PNEUMONIA

cards.treat: If coughing for 14 days or more refer for assessment; Soothe the throat and relieve cough with a safe remedy; Treat wheezing if present; Advise mother when to return immediately; Follow up in 5 days if not improving

read.text: “Up to” means the range that includes the first age and every age between, but not the last age. 2 months up to 12 months = 2, 3, 4 ... 11 months, but not 12 months. 12 months up to 5 years = 12 months, 24 months, 3 years, 4 years, but not 5 years.

Example: Fatima
Example:

Fatima is 18 months old. She weighs 11.5 kg, her length is 84 cm. Her temperature is 37.5°C. The health worker asked, "What are the child's problems?" The mother said, "Fatima has been coughing for 6 days, and she is having trouble breathing." This is the initial visit for this illness.

The health worker checked Fatima for general danger signs. The mother said that Fatima is able to drink. She has not been vomiting. She has not had convulsions during this illness. The health worker asked, "Does Fatima seem unusually sleepy?" The mother said, "Yes." The health worker clapped his hands. He asked the mother to shake the child. Fatima opened her eyes, but did not look around. The health worker talked to Fatima but she did not watch his face. She stared blankly and appeared not to notice what was going on around her.

The health worker asked the mother to lift Fatima's shirt. He then counted the number of breaths the child took in a minute. He counted 41 breaths per minute. The health worker did not see any chest indrawing. He did not hear stridor and he did not hear wheezing.
