cards.front: What are the steps for checking for general danger signs?
cards.back: Ask if the child is able to drink or breastfeed; ask if the child vomits everything; ask if the child has had convulsions; look to see if the child is convulsing now or lethargic or unconscious.

cards.front: How do you decide if the child vomits everything?
cards.back: The child is not able to keep anything down at all. What goes down comes back up.

cards.front: How do you decide if the child is lethargic?
cards.back: The lethargic child is sleepy when he should be awake. The child may stare blankly and appear not to see what is going on around him.

cards.front: How do you decide if the child is unconscious?
cards.back: The unconscious child does not waken at all. He does not respond to touch or to loud noises.

cards.front: What are the steps for assessing a child with cough or difficult breathing?
cards.back: Ask how long the child has been coughing; count the breaths in one minute and decide if the child has fast breathing; look for chest indrawing; look and listen for stridor.

cards.front: How do you recognize chest indrawing?
cards.back: The lower chest wall goes in when the child breathes IN. This should happen all the time.

cards.front: What should you do if you are not sure that chest indrawing is present?
cards.back: Ask the mother to change the child's position. If the lower chest wall does not go in when the child breathes in, the child does not have chest indrawing.
The child should be calm. Put your ear close to the child's mouth. Listen for a harsh noise when the child breathes IN.

sections.title: Diarrhoea: what it is, and its types

read.text: Say what diarrhoea is, and tell acute watery diarrhoea, persistent diarrhoea and dysentery apart.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 4.0 ASSESS AND CLASSIFY DIARRHOEA

Diarrhea: is the passage of unusually loose or watery stools, usually at least three times in a 24 hours’ period. It is common in children, especially those between 6 months and 2 years of age. It is more common in babies under 6 months who are drinking cow's milk or infant feeding formulas. Frequent passing of normal stools is not diarrhea. The number of stools normally passed in a day varies with the diet and age of the child. In many regions diarrhea is defined as three or more loose or watery stools in a 24-hour period.
Mothers usually know when their children have diarrhea. They may say that the child's stools are loose or watery. Mothers may use a local word for diarrhea.

Babies who are exclusively breastfed often have stools that are soft; this is not diarrhea. The mother of a breastfed baby can recognize diarrhea because the consistency or frequency of the stools is different from normal.
What are the Types of Diarrhea?
Most diarrheas which were causes dehydration are loose or watery. Cholera is one example of loose or watery diarrhea. Only a small proportion of all loose or watery diarrheas is due to cholera.

If an episode of diarrhea lasts less than 14 days, it is acute diarrhea. Acute watery diarrhea causes dehydration and contributes to malnutrition. The death of a child with acute diarrhea is usually due to dehydration.
If diarrhea lasts 14 days or more, it is diarrhea become persistent. Persistent contributes to deaths in children.

Up to 20% of episodes of diarrhea often causes nutritional problems and Diarrhea with blood in the stool, with or without mucus, is called dysentery. The most common cause of dysentery is Shigella bacteria. Amoebic dysentery is not common in young children. A child may have both watery diarrhea and dysentery.
Check yourself
Which type of diarrhoea?

items.text: An episode that lasts less than 14 days
Diarrhoea that lasts 14 days or more
Diarrhoea with blood in the stool, with or without mucus

read.text: A breastfed baby passes soft stools several times a day, as he always does. Does he have diarrhoea?
read.explanation: Babies who are exclusively breastfed often have stools that are soft; this is not diarrhea. Frequent passing of normal stools is not diarrhea.

read.text: Ask for diarrhea in ALL children:

items: ASK: Does the child have diarrhea? Use words for diarrhea the mother understands. If the mother answers NO, ask about the next main symptom, fever. You do not need to assess the child further for signs related to diarrhea then assess fever. If the mother answers YES, or if the mother said earlier that diarrhea was the reason for coming to the clinic, record her answer. Then assess the child for signs of dehydration, persistent diarrhea and dysentery.
ASK: For how long? Diarrhea, which lasts 14 days or more, is persistent diarrhea. Give the mother time to answer the question. She may need time to recall the exact number of days.
ASK: Is there blood in the stool? Ask the mother if she has seen blood in the stools at any time during this episode of diarrhea.

read.text: Check for signs of dehydration. When a child becomes dehydrated, he is at first thirsty restless and irritable. If dehydration continues, the child becomes lethargic or unconscious.
As the child's body loses fluids, the eyes may look sunken. When pinched, the skin will go back slowly or very slowly.
LOOK & FEEL for the following signs:

items: LOOK & FEEL for Child's general condition: Is the child lethargic or unconscious? Or Restless and irritable? Check to see if the child was lethargic or unconscious. If the child is lethargic or unconscious, he has a general danger sign. Remember to use this general danger sign when you classify the child's diarrhea. A child has the sign restless and irritable if the child is restless and irritable all the time or every time he is touched and handled. If an infant or child is calm when breastfeeding but again restless and irritable when he stops breastfeeding, he has the sign "restless and irritable". Many children are upset just because they are in the clinic. If these children can be consoled and calmed, they do not have the sign "restless and irritable".

LOOK for Sunken eyes: The eyes of a child who is dehydrated may look sunken. Decide if you think the eyes are sunken. Then ask the mother if she thinks her child's eyes look unusual. Her opinion helps you confirm that the child's eyes are sunken. Note: In a severely malnourished child who is visibly wasted (that is, who has marasmus), the eyes may always look sunken, even if the child is not dehydrated. Even though sunken eyes are less reliable in a visibly wasted child, still use the sign to the child's dehydration.

sections.title: Offer fluid and pinch the skin

read.text: Decide if a child is not able to drink, drinking poorly or drinking eagerly, and do a skin pinch.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text:
• OFFER the child fluid. Is the child not able to drink or drinking poorly? Drinking eagerly, thirsty? Ask the mother to offer the child some water in a cup or spoon. Watch the child drink. A child is not able to drink if he is not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink. A child may not be able to drink because he is lethargic or unconscious. A child is drinking poorly if the child is weak and cannot drink without help. He may be able to swallow only if fluid is put in his mouth. A child has the sign drinking eagerly, thirsty if it is clear that the child wants to drink. Look to see if the child reaches out for the cup or spoon when you offer him water. When the water is taken away, see if the child is unhappy because he wants to drink more. If the child takes a drink only with encouragement and does not want to drink more, he does not have the sign "drinking eagerly, thirsty."
  • PINCH the skin of the abdomen. Does it go back: slowly (less than 2seconds) or very slowly (longer than 2 seconds)? Ask the mother to place the child on the examining table so that the child is flat on his back with his arms at his sides (not over his head) and his legs straight. Or, ask the mother to hold the child so he is lying flat in her lap. Locate the area on the child’s abdomen halfway between the umbilicus and the side of the abdomen. To do the skin pinch, use your thumb and first finger. Do not use your fingertips because this will cause pain. Place your hand so that when you pinch the skin, the fold of skin will be in a line up and down the child's body and not across the child's body. Firmly pick up all of the layers of skin and the tissue under them. Pinch the skin for one second and then release it. When you release the skin, look to see if the skin pinch goes back:
    • Very slowly (longer than 2 seconds)
    • Slowly (less than 2 seconds)
    • Immediately Note: In a child with severe acute malnutrition, the skin may go back slowly even if the child is not dehydrated. In an overweight child, or a child with edema, the skin may go back immediately even if the child is dehydrated. Even though skin pinch is less reliable in these children, still use it to classify the child's dehydration.

read.text: 4.2 CLASSIFY DIARRHOEA
Diarrhea: is the passage of on usually loose or watery stools, usually at least three times in a 24 hours’ period.
There are three classification tables for classifying diarrhea.
All children with diarrhea are classified for:

items: Dehydration.
Persistent diarrhea if diarrhea for 14 days or more.
Dysentery If blood in the stool.

read.text: 4.2.1 Classify Dehydration
There are three possible classifications of dehydration in a child with diarrhea:

items: Severe dehydration usual fluid loss more than10% of body weight.

Some dehydration including moderate dehydration5-10%of body loss and mid dehydration 3- 5%of body loss both has the same signs of dehydration vary in severity but the health worker cannot differentiate.
No dehydration there is fluid loss but clinically not detectable less than 3% of body weight

cells: Two of the following signs: Lethargic or unconscious; Sunken eyes; Not able to drink or drinking poorly; Skin pinch goes back very slowly.
Two of the following signs: Restless, irritable; Sunken eyes; Drinks eagerly, thirsty; Skin pinch goes back slowly.
Not enough signs to classify as some or severe dehydration

sections.title: Fever: malaria, measles and other causes

read.text: Explain the common causes of fever in a sick child: malaria, measles, and fever with localizing, non-localizing signs or a rash.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 5.0 ASSESS AND CLASSIFY FEVER

A child with fever may have malaria, meningitis or measles or another severe diseases . A child with fever may have a bacterial infection such as pneumonia, acute ear infection, streptococcal sore throat, dysentery, local bacterial infection, typhoid, or urinary tract infection. Or, a child with fever may have a simple cough or cold or other viral infection.

For a health worker it is very important to identify key symptoms and signs of the diseases that may cause the child's death very quickly. Signs of a very severe disease may be general and non-specific, therefore all sick children with those signs should be referred to the hospital for further assessment and treatment.

All health workers should know how to assess a child for common childhood causes of fever, malaria or measles - two major killers of children under five in the world. In malaria risk areas, malaria is still a major cause of fever and death in children although measles has been on the decline due to successful measles immunization.
MALARIA:
A child has malaria and also cough with fast breathing. What does he need?
options: Treatment for both falciparum malaria and pneumonia
read.explanation: Signs of malaria can overlap with signs of other illness. This child needs treatment for both falciparum malaria and pneumonia.

read.text: Malaria is caused by parasites in the blood called “plasmodia.” They are transmitted through the bite of anopheles mosquitoes. Four species of plasmodia can cause malaria, but the only dangerous one is plasmodium falciparum. Other species that commonly causes malaria is Plasmodium vivax, which rarely causes very severe form but contributes to malaria morbidity in some countries. Malaria may occur throughout the year or during the rainy season in some countries. It is important to know when malaria occurs and which species cause it in your country or area of work.
Fever is the main symptom of malaria. It can be present all the time or go away and return at regular intervals. Other signs of malaria are shivering, sweating and vomiting.

Signs of malaria can overlap with signs of other illness. For example, a child may have malaria and cough with fast breathing, a sign of pneumonia. This child needs treatment for both falciparum malaria and pneumonia. Children with malaria may also have diarrhea. They need an antimalarial and treatment for the diarrhea.

In areas with very high malaria transmission, malaria is a major cause of death in children. A case of uncomplicated malaria can develop into severe malaria as soon as 24 hours after the fever first appears.
Severe malaria is malaria with complications such as cerebral malaria or severe anemia. The child can die if he does not receive urgent treatment.
How soon can uncomplicated malaria become severe malaria?
read.answer: A case of uncomplicated malaria can develop into severe malaria as soon as 24 hours after the fever first appears. Severe malaria is malaria with complications such as cerebral malaria or severe anemia; the child can die if he does not receive urgent treatment.

read.text: MEASLES:

Fever and a generalized rash are the main signs of measles. Measles is highly infectious. Maternal antibody protects young infants against measles for about 6 months. Then the protection gradually disappears. Measles cases occur in children between 6 months and 2 Years of age. Over-crowding and poor housing increase the risk of measles occurring early.

Measles is caused by a virus. It infects the skin and the layer of cells that line the lung, gut, eye, mouth and throat. The measles virus damages the immune system for many weeks or months after the onset of measles. This leaves the child at risk of other infections.
Complications of measles occur in about 30% of all cases. The most important are:

read.title: The complications of measles

cards.back: Severe eye infection (which may lead to corneal ulceration and blindness)

items: Encephalitis
Diarrhea (including dysentery and persistent diarrhea).
Pneumonia
Mouth ulcers
Ear infection
Severe eye infection (which may lead to corneal ulceration and blindness).

read.text: Note: Encephalitis (a brain infection) occurs in about one in thousand cases. A child with encephalitis may have a general danger sign such as convulsions or be lethargic or unconscious.

Measles contributes to malnutrition because it causes diarrhea, high fever and mouth ulcers. These problems interfere with feeding. Malnourished children are more likely to have severe complications due to measles. This is especially true for children who are deficient in vitamin A. One in ten severely malnourished children with measles may die. For this reason, it is very important to help the mother to continue feeding her child during measles.
Check yourself
Which is the only dangerous species of plasmodia, according to the book?
read.explanation: Four species of plasmodia can cause malaria, but the only dangerous one is plasmodium falciparum.

sections.title: Other causes of fever

read.text: Tell fever with localizing signs, with non-localizing signs and with a rash apart.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: OTHER CAUSES OF FEVER

• In a child with fever due to malaria, there should be malaria parasites or antigens when the blood is tested to confirm a malaria infection. If the child with fever has no malaria parasites or antigens, then it is unlikely that the fever is due to malaria.
  • There are three major categories of fever:
    • Fever with localizing signs.
    • Fever with non-localizing signs.
    • Fever with a rash.

Fever with localizing signs: A child might have an apparent cause of fever such as pneumonia, dysentery, meningitis, acute ear infection, sore throat or local bacterial infection, which have localizing signs that explain the infection that is causing fever.

Fever with non-localizing signs. A child might also have fever due to infection with no localizing signs to help you determine what is causing fever, like septicemia, typhoid fever, urinary tract infection, HIV infection or miliary tuberculosis. These infections are difficult to diagnose without laboratory tests and therefore children suspected of having these conditions should be referred to a hospital for assessment.

Fever with a rash. One of the common causes of fever with a rash is measles but it can also be another simple viral infection such as chicken pox or severe or infections like meningococcal meningitis and dengue hemorrhagic fever.

items: It is important to ask for all the main symptoms when assessing any sick child so that you can pick up the common and serious causes of fever.

It is also important to attempt to distinguish cases of possible bacterial causes of fever, which may require an antibiotic treatment, from cases of non-complicated viral infection. Signs of a bacterial infection may be a local tenderness, refusal to use a limb, hot tender swelling, red tender skin or boils, lower abdominal pain or pain on passing urine in older children.

read.text: ASK: Does the child have fever?

items: Ask and check if the child has a history of fever, feels hot or has a temperature of 37.5oC or above.
The child has a history of fever, if the child has had any fever with this illness.
Use words for ’fever’ that the mother understands. Make sure the mother understands what fever is. For example, ask the mother if the child’s body has felt hot.
Feel the child’s abdomen or axilla determine if the child feels hot.
Look to see if the child’s temperature was measured today and recorded on the child’s chart. If the child has a temperature of 37.5C or above, the child has fever.
If the child’s temperature has not been measured, and you have a thermometer, measure the child’s temperature.

If the child does not have fever (by history, feels hot or temperature 37.5oC or above), tick () NO on the Recording form. Ask about the next main symptom, ear problem. Do not assess the child for the signs related to fever.
Assess the child’s fever even if the child does not have a temperature of 37.5oC or above or does not feel hot now, history of fever is enough to assess the child for fever.

read.text: ASK: For how long? If fever more than 7 days; does it present every day?

Ask the mother how long the child has had fever. If the fever has been present for more than 7 days, ask if the fever has been present every day. Most fevers due to viral illnesses subside within a few days. A fever that has been present every day for more than 7 days can mean that the child has a more severe disease such as typhoid fever. Refer this child for further assessment.
ASK: Has the child had measles within the last 3 months?

Measles damages the child immune system and leaves the child at risk of other diseases for many weeks. A child with fever and a history of measles within the last 3 months may have an infection due to complications of measles such as an eye infection.
Check yourself

read.explanation: Assess the child's fever even if the child does not have a temperature of 37.5°C or above or does not feel hot now: history of fever is enough to assess the child for fever.

read.text: A child has had fever every day for 9 days. What can this mean?
options: A more severe disease such as typhoid fever: refer
read.explanation: A fever that has been present every day for more than 7 days can mean that the child has a more severe disease such as typhoid fever. Refer this child for further assessment.

sections.title: Look for stiff neck, the rash of measles, other causes, and do a malaria test

read.text: Check for stiff neck, recognise the generalized rash of measles, look for other causes of fever and decide when to do a malaria test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: LOOK AND FEEL: For the stiff neck.

A child with fever and stiff neck may have meningitis. A child with meningitis needs urgent treatment with injectable antibiotics and referral to a hospital. While you talk with the mother during the assessment, look to see if the child moves and bends his neck easily as he looks around. If the child is moving and bending his neck, he is not having a stiff neck. If you do not see any movement, or if you are not sure, draw the child’s attention to his umbilicus or toes. For example, you can shine a flashlight on his toes or umbilicus or tickle his toes to encourage the child to look down. Look to see if the child can bend his neck when he looks down at his umbilicus or toes. If you still have not seen the child bend his neck by himself, ask the mother to help you lay the child on his back. Lean over the child, gently support his back and shoulder with one hand. With the other hand, hold his head. Then carefully bend the head forward towards his chest. Another method can be used, when the child lies on his back with one hand hold his head, put the other hand on his chest and then carefully try to bend the head towards his chest. If the neck bends easily, the child does not have stiff neck. If the neck feels stiff and there is resistance to bending, the child has a stiff neck. Often a child with a stiff neck will cry when you try to bend the neck.
If the neck bends easily when you gently bend the head towards the chest, what does the child have?
read.explanation: If the neck bends easily, the child does not have stiff neck. If the neck feels stiff and there is resistance to bending, the child has a stiff neck.

read.text: LOOK for signs suggesting MEASLES

items: Generalized rash In measles, a red rash begins behind the ears and on the neck. It spreads to the face. During the next day, the rash spreads to the rest of the body, arms and legs. After 4 to 5 days, the rash starts to fade and the skin may peel. Some children with severe infection may have more rash spread over more of the body. The rash becomes more discolored (dark brown or blackish), and there is more peeling of the skin. A measles rash does not have vesicles (blisters) or pustules. The rash does not itch. Do not confuse measles with other common childhood rashes such as chicken box, scabies or heat rash. (The chicken box rash is a generalized rash with vesicles. scabies occurs on the hand, feet, ankles, elbows, buttocks and axilla. It also itches. Heat rash can be a generalized rash with small bumps and vesicles, which itch. (A child with heat rash is not sick.) You can recognize measles more easily during times when other cases of measles are occurring in your community.

read.text: Which rash does the book describe as measles?
options: A rash that itches and has blisters
A red rash that begins behind the ears and on the neck, spreads to the face and then the body, and does not itch
A rash on the hands, feet, ankles and elbows that itches
read.explanation: A measles rash does not have vesicles (blisters) or pustules. The rash does not itch. Chickenpox is a generalized rash with vesicles; scabies occurs on the hands, feet, ankles, elbows, buttocks and axilla and itches.

read.text: LOOK: for any other cause of fever

Assess the child for signs of any other infection that can cause fever . A runny nose in a child with fever may mean that the child has a common cold. Remember that an obvious cause of fever also includes a cough or difficulty breathing, classification DYSENTERY - a main symptom, which would have been already assessed- or an ear problem – the next main symptom that will be assessed-. Also, look for signs of possible bacterial infection: local tenderness, refusal to use a limb, hot tender swelling, red tender skin or boils. If the child is older, check if the child has lower abdominal pain or pain on passing urine. DO malaria test? It is not possible to clinically distinguish fever caused by malaria from other causes of fever because there are many causes of fever. To be sure that a child with a fever or history of fever has a malaria infection, you need to do a malaria test. Testing for malaria will also help in distinguishing malaria caused by P. falciparum from that caused by P. vivax. P. falciparum is the most dangerous.
A child with fever has a danger sign or a stiff neck. Do you do a malaria test first?
options: No: do not delay referral; give pre-referral antimalarial and antibiotic treatment and refer urgently
read.explanation: Do not do a malaria test if a child has a danger sign or a stiff neck to avoid delay in referral but give pre-referral antimalarial and antibiotic treatment, and refer the child urgently.

read.text:
• There are two ways of doing a malaria test:
    • Examining a blood slide for malaria parasites using a microscope.
    • Checking blood using a Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) for malaria antigens. When to do a malaria diagnostic test A malaria test should be done in all children with a fever or history of fever with No general danger signs or stiff neck. Do not do a malaria test if a child has a danger sign or a stiff neck to avoid delay in referral but give pre-referral antimalarial and antibiotic treatment, and refer the child urgently
  • Record the malaria test result to indicate:
  • POSITIVE - if there are malaria parasites or if the malaria test is positive. You should also note if it is
    • positive P. falciparum
    • Positive P. vivax
  • NEGATIVE - if you do not see parasites by microscopy or if the the malaria test is negative. Always check the quality of your blood slides if using microscopy or RDTs to ensure that the test results are reliable.

sections.title: Measles complications: mouth ulcers, and Exercise I

read.text: Look for mouth ulcers in a child with measles and tell them from Koplik spots.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: If the child has MEASLES now or within the last 3 months:
LOOK for measles complications

items: Measles complications may be mouth, eye, pneumonia, diarrhea, ear infection or malnutrition

Look to see if the child has mouth or eye complications. Other complications of measles such as stridor in a calm child, pneumonia, and diarrhea are assessed earlier; malnutrition and ear infection will be assessed later.

Look for mouth ulcers. Are they deep and extensive? Look inside the child’s mouth for mouth ulcer. Ulcers are painful open sores on the inside of the mouth and lips or the tongue. They may be red or have white coating on them. In severe cases, they are deep and extensive. When present, mouth ulcers make it difficult for the child with measles to drink or eat.

Mouth ulcers are different from the small spots called Koplik spots, Koplik spots occur in the mouth inside the cheek during early stages of the measles infection. Koplik spots are small, irregular, bright red spots with a white spot in the center. They do not interfere with drinking or eating. They do not need treatment.

sections.title: Measles complications: the eye, and Exercise J

read.text: Look for pus draining from the eye and clouding of the cornea.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: The eye
The normal eye consists of:

• The conjunctiva lines the eyelids and covers the white part of the eye. The iris is the colored part of the eye. The normal cornea (the clear window of the eye) is bright and transparent. Through it, you can see the iris and the round pupil at is middle. A normal cornea is clear. You can see the color of the iris clearly. The pupil is black.
  • In assessing the eye for measles complication LOOK:
  • For pus draining from the eye. Pus draining from the eye is a sign of conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis is an infection of the conjunctiva, the inside surface of the eyelid and the white part of the eye.
    • If you do not see pus draining from the eye, look for pus on the conjunctiva or on the eyelids.
    • Often the pus forms a crust when the child is sleeping and seals the eye shut. It can be gently opened with clean hands. Wash your hands after examining the eye of any child with pus draining from the eye.
  • For clouding of the cornea.
    • The cornea is usually clear. When clouding of the cornea is present, there is a hazy area in the cornea.
    • Look carefully at the cornea for clouding. The cornea may appear clouded or hazy, such as how a glass of water looks when you add a small amount of milk. The clouding may occur in one or both eyes.
    • Corneal clouding is a dangerous condition. The corneal clouding may be due to vitamin A deficiency, which has been made worse by measles. If the corneal clouding is not treated, the cornea can ulcerate and cause blindness. A child with clouding of the cornea needs urgent treatment with vitamin A.
    • A child with corneal clouding may keep his eye tightly shut when exposed to light. The light may cause irritation and pain to the child’s eyes. To check the child’s eye, wait for the child to open his eye. Or, gently pull down the lower eyelid to look for clouding.
    • If there is clouding of the cornea, ask the mother how long the clouding has been present. If the mother is certain that clouding has been there for some time, ask if the clouding has already been assessed and treated at the hospital. If it has, you do not need to refer this child again for corneal clouding.

sections.title: Example: how the health worker classified Tariq

read.text: Follow, step by step, how a health worker classifies a child's fever and measles.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: EXERCISE K
In this exercise, you will classify illness in children with signs of fever and, if present, signs suggesting measles. First, you will study an example. Then you will begin the exercise.

Read the example case study that begins on this page. Also, study how the health worker classified this child’s illness. When all the participants are ready, there will be a group discussion about this example.

EXAMPLE 1: Tariq Tariq is 10 months old. He weighs 8.2kg, Length 60cm. His temperature is 37.5o C. His mother says he has a rash and cough. The health worker checked Tariq for general danger signs. sections.title: Assess ear problem

read.text: Ask about ear pain and discharge, look for pus draining from the ear and feel for tender swelling behind the ear.

read.text: Pus has drained from a child's ear for 14 days. Acute or chronic?
feedback: Acute is less than 14 days.
Right. 14 days or more is chronic.

read.text: 6.0 ASSESS AND CLASSIFY EAR PROBLEM

A child with an ear problem may have an ear infection. When a child has an ear infection, pus collects behind the eardrum and causes pain and often fever. If the infection is not treated, the eardrum may burst. The pus discharges, and the child feels less pain. The fever and other symptoms may stop, but the child suffers from poor hearing because the eardrum has a hole in it. Usually the eardrum heals by itself. At other times the discharge continues, the eardrum does not heal, and the child becomes deaf in that ear.

Sometimes the infection can spread from the ear to the bone behind the ear (the mastoid) causing mastoiditis. Infection can also spread from the ear to the brain causing meningitis. These are severe diseases. They need urgent attention and referral.

Ear infections rarely cause death. However, they cause many days of illness in children. Ear infections are the main cause of deafness in developing countries, and deafness causes learning problems in school. The ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart helps you identify ear problems due to ear infection.
6.1 ASSESS EAR PROBLEM
A child with ear problem is assessed for:

items: Ear pain
Ear discharge, If discharge is present, how long the child has had discharge?
Tender swelling behind the ear, a sign of mastoiditis.

read.text:
The box below shows how to assess a child with ear problem

Does the child have an ear problem?                              Yes No
ASK:                                               LOOK AND FEEL
• Is there ear pain?                               Look for pus draining from the ear
• Is there ear discharge?                          Feel for tender swelling behind the ear
If yes, for how long      days

read.caption: The same box in your chart booklet.

read.text: Ask for ear problem in ALL sick children.
ASK: Does the child have an ear problem?
If the mother answers NO, record her answer. Do not assess the child for ear problem. Go to the next question and check for malnutrition and anemia.

items: If the mother answers YES, ask the next question:

read.text: ASK: Does the child have ear pain?
Ear pain can mean that the child has an ear infection. If the mother is not sure that the child has ear pain, ask if the child has been irritable and rubbing his ear.
ASK: Is there ear discharge? If yes, for how long?

Ear discharge is also a sign of infection. When asking about ear discharge, use words the mother understands. If the child has had ear discharge, ask for how long. Give her time to answer the question. She may need to remember when the discharge started.

items: You will classify and treat the ear problem depending on how long the ear discharge has been present:
An ear discharge that has been present for 2 weeks or more is treated as a chronic ear infection.
An ear discharge that has been present for less than 2 weeks is treated as an acute ear infection.
You do not need more accurate information about how long the discharge has been present. LOOK for pus draining from the ear.
Pus draining from the ear is a sign of infection, even if the child no longer has any pain.
Look inside the child's ear to see if pus is draining from the ear. FEEL for tender swelling behind the ear.
Feel behind both ears.
Compare them and decide if there is tender swelling of the mastoid bone. In infants, the swelling may be above the ear.
Both tenderness and swelling must be present to classify mastoiditis, a deep infection in the mastoid bone. Do not confuse this swelling of the bone with swollen lymph nodes.

read.text: Check yourself

read.explanation: Both tenderness and swelling must be present to classify mastoiditis. Do not confuse this swelling of the bone with swollen lymph nodes.

sections.title: Malnutrition and anaemia: why they matter

read.text: Explain acute malnutrition, severe acute malnutrition, RUTF, and the causes of anaemia.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 7.0 CHECK FOR MALNUTRITION
Malnutrition is associated with many childhood illnesses and deaths. There are several types of malnutrition.

One type of malnutrition is acute malnutrition. Acutely malnourished children lack growth nutrients that are required to build new tissues. These nutrients also aid weight gain after illness, repair damaged tissues and help replace the rapid turnover of cells (intestine and immune cells). Correct replenishment of nutrients is essential for recovery from malnutrition. A child who has had frequent illnesses can also develop acute malnutrition. The child's appetite decreases, and the food that the child eats is not used efficiently.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is a life-threatening condition requiring urgent treatment. Until recently, the recommendation was to refer children suffering from SAM to hospital to receive therapeutic diets along with medical care. Treating severely malnourished children in hospitals however, is not always desirable or practical especially in rural settings. The situation has changed with the advent of ready to use therapeutic foods (RUTF) which allows the management of a large numbers of children who are severely malnourished above the age of 6 months and without medical complications at home and they account 80% of cases of SAM .

RUTF is made according to a standard, energy-rich composition defined by the World Health Organization. Typically, RUTF is made from full-fat milk powder, sugar, peanut butter, vegetable oil, and vitamins and minerals. The benefits of RUTF include low moisture content, a long shelf life without needing refrigeration and that it requires no preparation.
A child whose diet lacks recommended amounts of essential vitamins and minerals can also develop malnutrition.
Not eating foods rich in iron can lead to iron deficiency and anemia. Anemia is a reduced number of red cells or a reduced amount of hemoglobin in each red cell.

A child can also develop anemia because of infection: parasites such as hookworm (Ancylostoma and Necator) or whipworm (Trichuris), which can cause blood loss from the gut. Malaria can destroy red cells rapidly.

Children can develop anemia if they have had repeated episodes of malaria or if the malaria was inadequately treated. The anemia may develop slowly. Often, anemia in these children is a result of both malnutrition and malaria.
Check yourself

Children with severe acute malnutrition and without medical complications, above the age of 6 months, can be managed at home with ready to use therapeutic food (RUTF). About what share of SAM cases are they?
read.explanation: They account 80% of cases of SAM.

read.text: Which can cause anaemia?
groups: Not a cause given in the book

items.text: Not eating foods rich in iron

sections.title: Assess for acute malnutrition: oedema and weight for length or height

read.text: Look and feel for oedema of both feet and determine weight for length or height.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: A child's MUAC is normal. Can she still have severe acute malnutrition?
options: Yes, if she has oedema of both feet or a very low weight for length
feedback: Check oedema of both feet and weight for length too.
Right. Check all three: oedema, WFH/L and MUAC.

read.text: 7.1 ASSESS FOR ACUTE MALNUTRITION
After assessing the child for general danger signs and the four main symptoms (cough or difficulty breathing, diarrhea, fever and ear problem) then assess all children for Acute Malnutrition

• Assess all children for Signs of acute malnutrition
    • Edema of both feet
    • WFH/L - weight for height (more than 2 years of age) or weight for length (up to 2 years of age)
    • Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) in children aged 6 months or more
  • In the presence of signs of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) check for any medical complications and assess appetite or breastfeeding when indicated.
LOOK and FEEL for edema of both feet:

A child with edema of both feet may have kwashiorkor, another form of severeacute malnutrition. Edema is when an unusually large amount of fluid gathers in the child's tissues. The tissues become filled with the fluid and look swollen or puffed up.

Look and feel to determine whether the child has edema of both fetes?. Use your thumb to press gently for a few seconds on the top side of each foot. The child has edema if a dent remains in the child's foot when you lift your thumb.

• classification of edema:
    • +on dorsum of food
    • ++up thigh
    • +++ generalized
ASSESS weight for height or length (WFH/L):

Assess the child's body weight in proportion to attained growth in heightor length.Look now at the example: WHO weight-for-length graph below. The line labeled zero is the median, which is generally speaking, the average. Most healthy children are near the median curve, a little either above or below it. The other lines, called z -score or standard deviations (SD) lines, indicate distance from the average. You will identify children whose weight for length or height is below -3 z-scores curve of the graph; it is the bottom curve of the graph. These children suffer from severe acute malnutrition. You will also identify children whose weight-for-height or length is between -2 and -3 z-scores. These children have moderate acute malnutrition.

• To determine weight-for-height or length:
    • Calculate the child's age in months.
    • Weigh the child (unless the child has already been weighed today). The child should wear light clothing when being weighed.
    • Measure length or height:
      • If a child is less than 2 years old, measure lying down (recumbent) length.
      • If the child is aged 2 years or older and able to stand, measure standing height.
  • NOTE: In general, standing height is about 0.7 cm less than lying down length. Therefore, if a child less than 2 years old will not lie down for measurement of length, measure standing height and add 0.7 cm to convert it to length; if a child aged 2 years or older cannot stand, measure lying down length and subtract 0.7 cm to convert it to Height.

read.caption: The WHO weight-for-length graph in the book. Use the charts in your chart booklet.

sections.title: MUAC, medical complications and the appetite test

read.text: Measure MUAC, check a child with severe acute malnutrition for medical complications, and do an appetite test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: MEASURE mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)
A quick way of identifying acute malnutrition in children aged 6 months and more is measuring the mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC).
To measure the mid upper arm circumference:

items: Use a special tape for measuring MUAC or, if not available, a string
Place the tape or string placed around the upper arm, midway between the tip of shoulder and the tip of bent elbow
Do not to pull the tape or string too tightly To obtain the mid upper arm circumference:
Read the measurement if you used a tape
Measure the string with a ruler if you used a string MUAC interpretation
If MUAC is less than 115 mm - severe acute malnutrition and threat of death
If MUAC is 115 up to 125 mm - moderate acute malnutrition
If MUAC is 125 mm or more – no malnutrition

read.text: CHECK for medical complications

Severely malnourished children who have also medical complications have a high risk of death and need to be treated in a hospital and usually less than 20%of cases of SAM. Check a child that has edema of both feet or MUAC less than 115 mm or WHF/L less than -3 z-scores for medical complications necessitating referral. Medical complications necessitating referral are:

items: Any general danger sign
Any severe classification
Pneumonia with chest indrawing Note: These complications include main symptoms, which would have been already assessed ASSESS appetite
An important criterion to decide if a child suffering from severe acute malnutrition can be treated at home or needs to be referred to a hospital is the appetite test.
Malnutrition changes the way infections and other diseases express themselves.

Children severely affected by infections or and other diseases, who are malnourished, frequently show no signs of these diseases. Major complications lead to a loss of appetite. A poor appetite means that the child has a significant infection or a major metabolic abnormality such as liver dysfunction, electrolyte imbalance, cell membrane damage, or damaged biochemical pathways. Such child is at immediate risk of death.

read.text: Conducting an appetite test means offering the child Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and assessing whether the child ate at least the amount described below. The appetite test is conducted at the initial visit and each follow-up visit to the health facility. The test usually takes a short time but may take up to 30 minutes.
Why does a poor appetite matter in a child with severe acute malnutrition?
read.answer: Major complications lead to a loss of appetite. A poor appetite means that the child has a significant infection or a major metabolic abnormality. Such a child is at immediate risk of death.

read.text: Conduct an appetite test for a child aged 6 months or more who:

• Has MUAC less than 115 mm OR
  • Has WFH/L less than -3 z- score OR
  • Has edema of both feet AND
  • Does NOT have medical complications. To conduct an appetite test
  • Arrange a quiet corner where the child and mother can take their time to get accustomed to eating the RUTF.
  • The child may not eat the RUTF because he or she is frightened, distressed or fearful of the environment or staff. This is particularly likely if there is a crowd, a lot of noise, other distressed children or intimidating health professionals (white coats, awe-inspiring tone). The appetite test should therefore be conducted a separate quiet area. If a quiet area is not possible then the appetite can be tested outside the clinic.
  • Determine RUFT portion needed to perform the test (1/3 RUTF scatch 92 gram)
  • Explain to the mother:
    • Your child is malnourished and needs to eat the Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) until he or she will grow well again. RUTF is a food and medicine for malnourished children and show her photos of transformation before and after illness.
    • I need to see if your child has a good appetite and will eat the RUTF in sufficient amounts at home. Therefore, I will give you some RUTF and you will feed it to your child now.
  • Advise the mother to:
    • Wash hands before giving the RUTF
    • Sit with the child on her lap and gently offer the child RUTF to eat.
    • Encourage the child to eat the RUTF. If the child refuses, continue to quietly encourage the child and take your time. Do not force the child to eat the RUTF
    • Offer plenty of clean water to drink from a cup when the child is taking the RUTF.
  • After 30 minutes asses the results of appetite test:
  • A child that eat 1/3 amount of RUFT scatch , Pass the appetite test.
  • Now explain to the mother that the child can be treated at home. You will learn how to explain to her how to feed the child at home and when to return for the follow-up visit later in this training.
  • A child that does NOT eat 1/3 amount of RUFT scatch, fails the appetite test.
  • Explain now to the mother that her child needs to eat the RUTF to treat his orher malnutrition but because of poor appetite the child would not take sufficient amounts of the RUTF at home, would continue to get worse, and could even die. For this reason, the child needs to be urgently treated in a hospital. Even if you or the mother think that the child did not take the RUTF because he or she does not like the taste or is frightened, the child still needs to be referred to in-patient care for least a short time. If it is later found that the child actually takes sufficient RUTF to pass the test then he or she can be immediately transferred to the outpatient treatment.

sections.title: Classify nutritional status

read.text: Classify COMPLICATED SAM, UNCOMPLICATED SAM, MAM or NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION.

read.text: 7.2 CLASSIFICATION OF NUTRITIONAL STATUS
Based on the presence or absence of edema of both feet, WFH/L, and/or MUAC (in a child 6 months or older), the child’s condition can be classified as:

items: Complicated Severe acute malnutrition(SAM),
Un-complicated sever acute malnutrition
Moderate acute malnutrition(MAM), or
No acute malnutrition.

read.text: A child classified as severe acute malnutrition based on WFH/L, and/or MUAC is classified further as complicated severe acute malnutrition or uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition based on the presence or absence of medical complications and, depending on the age, the results of appetite test or breastfeeding assessment
COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION (SAM)

A child with edema of both feet is classified as having COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION. A child with WFH/L less than -3 z-scores or MUAC less than 115 mm with a medical complication or not able to finish RUTF if aged 6 months or more or having a breastfeeding problem if aged less than 6 months, is classified as having COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION.
UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION (SAM)
A child with WFH/L less than -3 z-scores or MUAC less than 115 mm and able to finish RUTF is classified as having UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION.
MODERATE ACUTE MALNUTRITION(MAM)
A child with WFH/L between -3 z and -2 z-scores or MUAC 115 up to 124 mm is classified as having MODERATE ACUTE MALNUTRITION.
NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION
A child with WFH/L -2 z-scores or more or MUAC 125 mm or more is classified as having NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION.

WFH/L between -3 and -2 Z-scores or MUAC 115 up to 125 mm

sections.title: Assess and classify anaemia

read.text: Look for palmar pallor and classify SEVERE ANAEMIA, ANAEMIA or NO ANAEMIA.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: How do you look for palmar pallor?
options: Compare the child's palm with your own
feedback: Right.
Look yourself.
IMNCI uses the palm.

read.text: 8.0 ASSESS AND CLASSIFY ANEMIA

Pallor is unusual paleness of the skin. It is a sign of anemia. Although this clinical sign is less reliable than many other clinical signs, it allows health-care providers to identify sick children with severe anemia, often caused by malaria infection. Where feasible, the specificity of anemia diagnosis may be greatly increased by using a simple laboratory test (e.g. Hb test).
8.1 ASSESS FOR ANEMIA
LOOK for palmar pallor:

items: To see if the child has palmar pallor, look at the skin of the child's palm. Hold the child's palm open by grasping it gently from the side. Do not stretch the fingers backwards, because this may cause pallor by blocking the blood supply.

Compare the color of the child's palm with your own palm and with the palms of other children. If the skin of the child's palm is pale, the child has some palmar pallor. If the skin of the palm is so pale that it looks white, the child has severe palmar pallor.

read.text: 8.2 CLASSIFICATION OF ANAEMIA
SEVERE ANAEMIA
If the child has severe palmar pallor, classify the child as having SEVERE ANAEMIA.
ANAEMIA
If the child has some palmar pallor, classify the child as having ANAEMIA.
NO ANAEMIA
If the child does not have palmar pallor, classify the child as having NO ANAEMIA
Classification table for Anemia

sections.title: Check the child's immunization status

read.text: Use the national schedule to decide which immunizations a sick child needs today.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 9.0 CHECK THE CHILD'S IMMUNIZATION AND VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION STATUS
9.1 CHECK THE CHILD’S IMMUNIZATION STATUS

Check the immunization status for ALL sick children. Have they received all the immunizations recommended for their age? Do they in need of any immunizations? use a recommended immunization schedule Use National recommended immunization schedule when you check the child's immunization status. Look at the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart and locate the recommended immunization schedule. Refer to it as you read how to check a child's immunization status. Most of the health facilities do not provide vaccines on daily basis. Vaccines in these health facilities are provided on scheduled days. Some other health facilities do not have vaccination service at all. Vaccination is provided within nearby health facility or by an out reaches service. The health worker should check the child’s immunization status and according to the situation within the health facility he will

items: Either give the immunization in the same day, or
Advise and direct the mother to where immunization is provided, or.
Direct the team to children who need immunization.

read.text: Check for vaccination and vitamin A supplementation (check on given vaccine and circle missed vaccine)

AgeVaccines
At birthOPV 0, BCG
6 weeksOPV 1, Rota 1, PCV 1, Penta 1, IPV 1
10 weeksOPV 2, Rota 2, PCV 2, Penta 2
14 weeksOPV3, Rota 3, PCV 3, Penta 3, IPV 2
9 monthsMeasles, Yellow fever, Men A
18 monthsMeasles boaster

read.caption: The immunization section of the Recording Form.

read.text: Record the recommended vaccine when the child age is appropriate for each dose. If the child receives an immunization when the child is too young, the child's body will not be able to fight the disease very well. In addition, if the child does not receive an immunization as soon as he is old enough, his risk of getting the disease increases. All children should receive all the recommended immunizations before their first birthday. If the child does not come for an immunization at the recommended age, give the necessary immunizations any time after the child reaches that age. Give the remaining doses at least 4 weeks apart. You do not need to repeat the whole schedule.
Check yourself
A child 5 months old has had only BCG and OPV 0. What do you do?
options: Give the immunizations he needs now; give the remaining doses at least 4 weeks apart
read.explanation: Give the necessary immunizations any time after the child reaches that age. Give the remaining doses at least 4 weeks apart. You do not need to repeat the whole schedule.

sections.title: Contraindications to immunization

read.text: Know the only three contraindications, and immunize sick children who are well enough to go home.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: OBSERVE CONTRAINDICATIONS TO IMMUNIZATION

In the past, some health workers thought minor illness was a contraindication to immunization (a reason to not immunize the child). They sent sick children away and told the mothers to bring them back when the children are well. This is a bad practice because it delays immunization. The mother may have traveled a long distance to bring her sick child to the clinic and cannot easily bring the child back for immunization at another time. The child is left at risk of getting measles, hepatitis B, Meningitis, polio, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus or tuberculosis.
It is very important to immunize sick and malnourished children against these diseases.
There are only three situations at present, which are contraindications to immunization:
Is it a contraindication to immunization? Sort each one the way the book says.

items.text: BCG for a child known to have AIDS
Penta 2 or Penta 3 for a child who had convulsions or shock within 3 days of the most recent dose
Penta for a child with recurrent convulsions or another active neurological disease of the central nervous system
A sick child who is well enough to go home

read.explanation: There are only three contraindications. There are no contraindications to immunization of a sick child if the child is well enough to go home.

items: 1- Do not give BCG to a child known to have AIDS.
2- Do not give Penta 2 or Penta 3 to a child who has had convulsions or shock within 3 days of the most recent dose.
3- Do not give Penta to a child with recurrent convulsions or another active neurological disease of the central nervous system.

read.text: Note: If DT and HB vaccine are available, given to children in the situation 2 and 3, because most complications of Penta vaccine are associated with pertussis vaccine.

• In all other situations, here is a good rule to follow:
    • There are no contraindications to immunization of a sick child if the Child is well enough to go home.
    • If a child is going to be referred, do not immunize the child before referral. The hospital staff at the referral site should make the decision about immunizing the child when the child is admitted. This will avoid delaying referral.
    • Children with diarrhea who are due for OPV should receive a dose of OPV (oral polio vaccine) during this visit. However, do not count the dose. The child should return in 4 weeks for an extra dose of OPV.
    • Advise the mother to be sure the other children in the family are immunized. Give the mother tetanus toxoid, if required.
    • To decide if the child needs an immunization:
LOOK at the child's age on the clinical record. If you do not already know the child's age, ask about the child's age. ASK the mother if the young infant has an immunization card.

items: If the mother answers YES:
Ask her if she has brought the card to the clinic today.
If she has brought the card with her, ask to see the card.
Compare the young infant immunization record with the recommended immunization schedule. Decide whether the young infant has had all the immunizations recommended for the child's age.
On the Recording Form, check all immunizations the young infant has already received.
Write the date of the immunization the child received most recently. Circle any immunization the child needs.
If the child is not being referred, explain to the mother that the child needs to receive an immunization (or immunizations).
If the mother says that she does NOT have an immunization card with her:
Ask the mother to tell you what immunizations the child has received.
Use your judgment to decide if the mother has given a reliable report. If you have any doubt, immunize the child.
Give an immunization card to the mother and ask her to please bring it with her

sections.title: Check the child's vitamin A supplementation status

read.text: Decide if a child needs vitamin A today.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 8.2 CHECK THE CHILD’S VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION STATUS
Vitamin A is given both to treat and to prevent disease.

items: It is given as treatment to children with measles, or severe malnutrition.
It is given as supplementation to prevent vitamin A deficiency

read.text: Many children in Sudan have some degree of vitamin A deficiency, which does not show. Therefore, giving vitamin A to all children age 6 months or older will prevent vitamin A deficiency. This will of course include children with persistent diarrhea, malnutrition, pneumonia and other illness. In several studies, this approach has been shown to reduce mortality in areas with vitamin A deficiency. Another important way to prevent deficiency is to make sure that infants are breastfed and, that after 6 months of age; they are fed complementary foods, which are rich in vitamin A.
When giving vitamin A as a supplement to prevent deficiency, make sure that it is not given more often than every 6 months.
Record the date on which the vitamin A dose was given on the child’s card.

When supplies of vitamin A are adequate, all children age 6 months up to 5 years should receive vitamin A every 6 months. Visits to clinic for illness are an opportunity to check when the child most recently received vitamin A. If the child is age 6 months or older and has not received vitamin A in the previous 6 months, give a single dose of vitamin A in the clinic.
Giving vitamin A for treatment of measles or severe malnutrition is the most important use. If vitamin A supplies are limited, use what vitamin A you have to treat children with these illnesses.
VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION STATUS:
Is child age 6 months or older? Has child received a dose of vitamin A in the previous 6 months?
To check the child’s vitamin A supplementation status:

• Look at the child’s age. You will only give vitamin A supplementation if the child is 6 months or older.
  • Look at the child’s card:
    • See if there is a record of previous vitamin A doses.
    • If no vitamin A has been given in the last 6 months, the child should receive a dose.
    • Circle the Vitamin A Supplementation box on the Recording Form.
Check yourself
A child 10 months old received vitamin A 2 months ago. Does he need vitamin A supplementation today?
read.explanation: When giving vitamin A as a supplement to prevent deficiency, make sure that it is not given more often than every 6 months.

read.text: A child 4 months old has never had vitamin A. Does he need vitamin A supplementation today?
read.explanation: You will only give vitamin A supplementation if the child is 6 months or older.

read.text: Assess any other problems, and remember that a child with any danger sign is referred.

read.text: 10.0 ASSESS OTHER PROBLEMS

items: The last box on the ASSESS side of the chart reminds you to assess any other problems that the child may have.

Since the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart does not address all of a sick child's problems, you will now assess other problems the mother told you about. For example, she may have said the child has a skin infection, itching or swollen neck glands. Or you may have observed another problem during the assessment. Identify and treat any other problems according to your training, experience and clinic policy. Refer the child for any other problem you cannot manage in clinic.
The last box on the "Classify" side of the chart has an important warning. It says:

read.text: MAKE SURE CHILD WITH ANY DANGER SIGN IS REFERRED after first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and other urgent treatments. Exception: Rehydration of the child according to Plan C may resolve danger signs so that referral is no longer needed.

items: This note reminds you that a child with any general danger sign needs urgent treatment and referral. It is possible, though uncommon, that a child may have a general danger sign, but may not have a severe classification for any of the main symptoms. How to decide and plan for referral of a child with a general danger sign and without any other severe classification is taught in the module Identify Treatment.

What you learned

  • Check every sick child for the general danger signs first.
  • Not able to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious, convulsing now.

sections.title: Introduction to identify treatment

read.text: Say what this module teaches: deciding on urgent referral and identifying the treatments a sick child needs.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Identify treatment: an overview
read.caption: The narration is being recorded.

read.text:
• 1. Introduction In the previous module you learned to assess the sick child age 2 months up to 5years and to classify the child's illness or illnesses. The next step is to identify the necessary treatments. In some instances, the very sick child will need referral to a hospital for additional care. If so, you will begin urgent treatments before the child's departure.
  • 2. Learning objectives This module will describe and allow you to practice the following skills:
  • determining if urgent referral is needed
  • identifying treatments needed
  • For patients who need urgent referral:
    • identifying the urgent pre-referral treatments
    • explaining the need for referral to the mother
    • writing the referral note
This module will focus on identifying which treatments are needed. The next module, Treat Child, will teach how to give the treatments.

This module describes the final step on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart: Identify Treatment. Read across the chart from each classification to the list of treatments needed. For example, find PNEUMONIA and read its treatments; then diarrhoea with NO DEHYDRATION; then DYSENTERY. Severe classifications usually require referral: “Refer URGENTLY to hospital”. This module does not describe how to do the treatments, only how to identify which treatments are needed.
read.label: From your facilitator

   GIVE FOLLOW UP CARE WHEN THE INFANT OR CHILD RETURN TO THE
        CLINICS AND IF NECESSERY REASSESS FOR NEW PROBLEM

In this module you will use the "identify Treatment" column of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart. If a child has only one classification, it is easy to see what to do for the child. However, many children have more than one classification

When a child has more than one classification, you must look at more than one place on the ASSESS and CLASSIFY chart to see the treatments listed. The coloured rows help you to quickly identify treatment.
A classification in a pink row means that the child needs urgent referral or admission for inpatient care. This is a severe classification

A classification in a yellow row means that the child needs an appropriate oral drug or other treatment. The treatment includes teaching the mother how to give oral drugs or to treat local infections at home. You also must advise her about caring for the child at home and when she should return

A classification in a green row means that the child does not need specific medical treatment such as antibiotics. Teach the child's caretaker how to care for the child at home. For example, you might advise her on feeding her sick child or giving fluid for diarrhoea. Then teach her signs indicating when the child should return immediately to the health facility

For some classifications, the treatment column says: "Refer urgently to hospital." Hospital means a health facility with inpatient beds, supplies and expertise to treat a very sick child. If your health facility has inpatient beds, referral may mean admission to the inpatient department of that facility. If an infant or child must be referred urgently, you must decide which treatments to do before referral. Some treatments (such as wicking an ear) are not necessary before referral. This section will help you to identify urgent pre-referral treatments

If there is no hospital in the area, you may make some decisions differently than as described in this unit. If referral is not possible, or if the parents refuse to take the child to the hospital, you should help the family care for the child. The child may stay near the clinic to be seen several times a day. Or a health worker may visit the home to help give drugs on schedule and to help give fluids and food
NOTE: There is an annex in the module Treat the Child, which explains what to do when referral is needed but not possible.

Look at the severe classifications on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart. These are coloured in pink and include:

read.text: Notice the instruction “Refer URGENTLY to hospital” in the lists of treatments for these classifications. This instruction means to refer the child immediately after giving any necessary pre- referral treatments. Do not give treatments that would unnecessarily delay referral.

Exception: For SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA, the instruction is simply “Refer to hospital.” This means that referral is needed, but not as urgently. There is time to identify treatments as described in section 2.0 of this module and give all of the treatments before referral. You may keep and treat a child whose only severe classification is SEVERE DEHYDRATION if your clinic has the ability to treat the child. sections.title: Referral for general danger signs and other severe problems

read.text: Refer a child with a general danger sign and no severe classification, or with another severe problem you cannot treat.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 3.2 Referral for general danger signs
Most children who have a general danger sign also have a severe classification. They will be referred for their severe classification (or possibly treated if they have SEVERE DEHYDRATION only).

In rare instances, children may have general danger signs without a severe classification. These children should be referred urgently. There is a box at the bottom of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart to remind you:
MAKE SURE A CHILD WITH ANY GENERAL DANGER SIGN IS

REFERRED after first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and other urgent pre-referral treatments. Exception: Rehydration of the child according to Plan C may resolve danger signs so that referral is no longer needed.
REFERRAL FOR OTHER SEVERE PROBLEMS
The ASSESS and CLASSIFY chart does not include all problems that children may have. You must ask yourself:
Does the child have any other severe problem that cannot be treated in this clinic?
For example, the child may have a severe problem that is not covered on the chart, such as severe abdominal pain. If you cannot treat a severe problem, you will need to refer the child.

Remember: Most children will have none of the general danger signs, severe classification, or other severe problems. If the child has none of these, the child dose not need urgent referral to a hospital. You will identify treatments needed as described in section 4.0 of this module.
Check yourself
A child has a general danger sign but no severe classification. What do you do?
options: Refer urgently after the first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and other urgent treatments
read.explanation: MAKE SURE A CHILD WITH ANY GENERAL DANGER SIGN IS REFERRED after first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and other urgent pre-referral treatments.

sections.title: Identify treatments for children who do not need urgent referral

read.text: List each treatment needed on the back of the Recording Form, with the earliest definite follow-up.
read.label: In this lesson

items: 4. Identify treatments for patients who do not need urgent referral

read.text: Your facilitator will present the example in this section and will show you how to use the back of the Sick Child Recording Form. The facilitator will show you how to: Fold the "classify" column of the Sick Child Recording Form so that you can see it while looking at the back of the form.
4.1 Identify treatment
Look at the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart to find the treatments needed for each of the child's classifications. List each treatment needed on the back of the Sick Child Recording Form

For each classification listed on the front of the Sick Child’s Recording Form, you will write the treatments needed on the back of the form. The treatments that may be needed are in the "Identify Treatment" column of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart. You will list only the treatments that apply to the specific child being treated.

Be sure to include items that begin with the words "Follow-up." These mean to tell the mother to return in a certain number of days. The follow-up visit is very important to see if the treatment is working or not, and give another treatment if needed. You may abbreviate follow-up as "F/up."

If several different times are specified for follow-up, you will look for the earliest definite time. (A definite time is one that is not followed by the word "if"). For example: "Follow-up in 3 days" gives a definite time for follow-up. "Follow-up in 3 days if fever persists" is not definite. The child only needs to come back if fever persists.

Record the earliest definite time for follow-up in the appropriate space on the back of the Sick Child Recording Form. This is the follow-up visit to tell the mother about. (Also tell her about any earlier follow-up that may be needed if a condition such as fever persists.) Later, when the mother returns for follow-up, you can tell her about any additional visits needed.

Also be sure to list non-urgent referrals for further assessment. For example, for cough which has lasted more than 14 days, or for fever, which has lasted 7 days or more, you would record, "Refer for assessment." Although the mother should take the child for assessment promptly, these causes of referral are not so urgent. Any other necessary treatments may be done before referral. You must teach the mother when to return immediately according to the appropriate classification and list them on the recording form. You will need to teach each mother the signs that mean she should return immediately for more care for her child. You will learn these signs later in this module. Note: you will learn to complete the feeding sections of the Sick Child Recording Form in the module COUNSEL THE MOTHER. When feeding assessment is needed, it may be done at any convenient time during the visit, after the child's immediate needs are taken care of. Some treatments are listed for more than one problem. If a patient has two problems that needed the same drug, you need only to the write the drug once on your Sick Child Recording Form. However, if an antibiotic is needed for more than one problem, you should list it each time. When the same antibiotic is appropriate for two different problems, you can give that single antibiotic, but two problems may require different antibiotics. You will learn about choosing antibiotics in the Treat the Child.
Most instructions in the "Identify Treatment" column of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart are easily understood. However, there are some instructions that require special explanation:

items: ANAEMIA A child with palmer pallor should begin iron treatment for ANAEMIA (make sure that the child has no sickle cell anemia and not receive RUTF). Give mebendazole if child is 1 year or older.

read.text: Fold the “Classify” column of the Recording Form so that you can see it while looking at the back. List the treatments across from each classification. Write only the relevant treatments. “Advise mother when to return immediately” is already printed on the form, so do not list it again. If you list several follow-up times, tell the mother the earliest definite time and record it in the space on the form.

sections.title: When to return immediately, and Exercise C

read.text: Teach the mother the signs that mean she must return immediately.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: 4.2 When to return immediately:

For all children going home, you will advise mother when to return immediately. This means to teach the mother certain signs that mean to return immediately for further care if the sick child develops one of them or more. These signs are listed on the COUNSEL THE MOTHER chart in the section WHEN TO RETURN. Use local terms that the mother will understand.
Tell every mother to return immediately if her child:

items: Is Not able to drink or breastfeed,
Becomes sicker, or
Develops fever.

read.text: Exception: If a child already has fever, you do not need to tell the mother to return immediately for fever.
Tell the mother of a child with simple cough or cold to watch for the following signs that mean the child may have developed pneumonia:

items: Fast breathing.
Difficult breathing.

read.text: Carefully explain these signs of possible pneumonia. If mothers do not understand the importance of these signs, they may not return when the child develops pneumonia, and the child may die.
Advise mothers of children with diarrhoea to watch for:

items: Blood in the stool
Poor drinking

read.text: Exception: If the child already has blood in the stool, you do not need to the mother to return immediately for blood, just for drinking poorly.
Which signs do you teach this mother?

items.text: Not able to drink or breastfeed

sections.title: Identify urgent pre-referral treatments

read.text: Identify the urgent treatments to give before referral, and the ones that must not delay it.
read.label: In this lesson

items: 5. Identify treatment if urgent referral is needed

read.text: 5.1 identify urgent pre-referral treatment needed

When a child needs urgent referral, you must quickly identify and begin the most urgent treatments for that child. The following are urgent treatments. They are in bold print on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart, you will give just the first dose of the drugs before referral:

items: Give diazepam to a child who is convulsing now.
Give quinine for VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE.
Give an appropriate antibiotic.
Give vitamin A for treatment of measles.
Treat the child to prevent low blood sugar (This involves giving breast milk, milk, or sugary water as described on the TREAT chart.)
Give rapid bronchodilator to treat wheeze.
Give paracetamol for high fever (38.5°C or above) or pain from mastoiditis.
Apply tetracycline eye ointment (if clouding of the cornea or pus draining from eye)
Provide ORS solution so that the mother can give frequent sips on the way to the hospital.

read.text: The first six treatments above are urgent because they can prevent serious consequences such as progression of bacterial meningitis or cerebral malaria, corneal rupture due to lack of vitamin A, or brain damage from low blood sugar or low oxygen level. The other listed treatments are also important to prevent worsening of the illness.

Do not delay referral to give non-urgent treatments such as wicking the ear or oral iron treatment. If immunizations or vitamin A supplementation are needed, do not give it before referral. Let hospital personnel to determine when to give immunizations and vitamin A supplement for prevention. This will avoid delaying referral. Give vitamin A when it is needed for treatment of a child with MEASLES.
EXAMPLE:

Nagla is a 15-month-old girl. She has COUGH OR COLD. She has fever of 38.2°C and stiff neck, so she is classified as having VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE, NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION AND NO ANEMIA and has no other classifications.
Nagla needs urgent referral. Before going to the hospital, she should be given:

items: Quinine (first dose).
Appropriate antibiotic (first dose).
Treatment to prevent low blood sugar.

read.text: The health worker should NOT take time to teach how to soothe the throat and relieve the cough with a safe remedy since that is not an urgent treatment. The health worker should NOT take time to assess feeding and counsel the mother on feeding.
